description_full: Children are already experts at asking why. Big Questions Club gives that curiosity a place to grow through stories, puzzles, mystery objects, movement, drawing, and role-play. As students explore questions about fairness, friendship, rules, and how we know what is true, they learn to explain what they think, listen to ideas, and discover how a thoughtful question can lead somewhere unexpected. Each day turns one big idea into something students can see and do. They might act out ways to share materials, follow instructions like a paper robot, sort clues to decide what can be known, or build a gallery around what makes something beautiful. Students can participate through speaking, drawing, acting, or building, making the course welcoming to different ways of participating. In the final week, each student chooses a favorite question and creates a Big Questions Gallery project. A poster, comic, model, or interactive display presents two possible answers, the student’s current view, and the reasons behind it. Students also complete an illustrated Big Questions journal and share their finished work in a supportive setting. This three-week course is part of Summer Discovery’s Institute for the Gifted program on Bryn Mawr College’s campus in Bryn Mawr, Pennsylvania. The program is available to commuter students. Beyond class, students take part in campus activities, make new friends, and build confidence trying something new.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Turn stories, mystery objects, and everyday choices into big questions • Explore fairness by sharing materials and acting out different solutions • Use clues, pictures, and playful puzzles to decide what they know and why • Act like a paper robot to ask whether following rules is the same as thinking • Share ideas through speaking, drawing, building, and respectful conversation • Create a poster, comic, model, or interactive Big Questions Gallery project

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Recognize when a question may have more than one thoughtful answer • Explain an idea using a reason, example, picture, or observation • Listen to and compare different viewpoints during a group conversation Students will leave with an illustrated Big Questions journal and a creative gallery project, plus stronger reasoning skills and curiosity to keep exploring.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for elementary school students who have completed 1st, 2nd, or 3rd grade and enjoy asking “why,” listening to stories, solving puzzles, drawing, building, or acting out choices. It is a good fit for curious talkers and quiet observers alike. Students can share ideas through words, pictures, movement, or models. They should be ready to listen, take turns, work with classmates, and share a finished project in a supportive setting. View the eligibility requirements for the Institute for the Gifted on our FAQ page. A completed program application is required.

learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Recognize when a question may have more than one thoughtful answer • Explain an idea using a reason, example, picture, or observation • Listen to and compare different viewpoints during a group conversation Students will leave with an illustrated Big Questions journal and a creative gallery project, plus stronger reasoning skills and curiosity to keep exploring.

description_full: How would you design a replacement body part that must fit, move and work with a real patient? Students begin by building a life-size anatomy model, then investigate how stem cells, medical devices and engineering can help repair or replace damaged tissues and organs. Design challenges make each body system concrete. Teams develop a prosthetic limb, map how 3D printing supports artificial organs and compare treatment options for kidney failure. They build and test an artificial heart valve, model lungs, investigate liver function and create an ear trumpet while considering hearing technology. Vision simulations and a cochlear-implant discussion add patient experience and ethics to the engineering work. Students document designs and reflections in a science journal while building a capstone proposal for a new application of regenerative medicine. The final project explains the medical need, proposed solution, possible benefits and drawbacks, and connections to areas such as cost, law, education or technology. Students choose a presentation format and share the finished proposal with the class. This three-week course is part of Summer Discovery’s Institute for the Gifted program on Bryn Mawr College’s campus in Bryn Mawr, Pennsylvania. The program is available to commuter students. Beyond class, students take part in campus activities, make new friends, and build confidence and independence in a college setting.

curriculum_sections.body: "• Build a life-size body model and connect organs to their functions • Design a prosthetic limb and evaluate its materials and constraints • Research 3D-printed organs and compare kidney-failure treatments • Construct and test an artificial heart valve and lung model • Explore vision, hearing and cochlear-implant questions through simulations and discussion • Propose and present a new regenerative-medicine application"

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain how selected organs function and how a medical device may support them • Apply an engineering design process to build and evaluate biomedical prototypes • Present a regenerative-medicine proposal that considers benefits, limits and wider effects Students will leave with a course completion certificate, a science journal, several biomedical models and a capstone proposal, plus a clearer sense of what they may want to explore across medicine and engineering.

Students should be ready to collaborate on prototypes, record observations, discuss patient and ethical questions respectfully, and develop a project across several checkpoints. The experience can help students identify which medical or engineering questions they want to explore next. View the eligibility requirements for the Institute for the Gifted on our FAQ page. A completed program application is required.

description_full: A secret message is a mathematical puzzle with a purpose. Students trace cryptography from Caesar shifts and substitution systems to the Enigma machine and the public-key ideas that protect modern communication. Each new cipher reveals both an encoding strategy and a weakness a codebreaker can exploit. Hands-on challenges include building cipher wheels, encrypting and decrypting partner messages, using frequency analysis, and testing Vigenère and Polybius-based systems. Students connect those activities to modular arithmetic, matrices, prime factorization, number theory, and the way computers represent information. Historical cases show how cryptanalysis influenced events and how security standards change when technology advances. For the capstone, students design and analyze an original cryptographic system or complete an in-depth cryptanalysis project. They document the key, method, mathematical reasoning, strengths, limitations, and evidence from testing, then present their findings to the class. This three-week course is part of Summer Discovery’s Institute for the Gifted program on Bryn Mawr College’s campus in Bryn Mawr, Pennsylvania. The program is available to commuter students. Beyond class, students take part in campus activities, make new friends, and build confidence and independence in a college setting.

curriculum_sections.body: • Encrypt and decrypt messages with Caesar and substitution ciphers • Use frequency analysis to test and break simple systems • Explore Vigenère, Polybius, Enigma, and public-key ideas • Apply modular arithmetic, matrices, primes, and number theory • Compare cipher strengths, weaknesses, and historical consequences • Design or analyze a cryptographic system for a final presentation

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain how major classical and modern cryptographic ideas protect information • Apply mathematical patterns and frequency evidence to encrypt or break messages • Design, test, and present an original cipher or cryptanalysis project Students will leave with encrypted work, documented codebreaking strategies, and a capstone that demonstrates mathematical reasoning and security analysis.

description_full: Why does a plant have tall stems, purple flowers or jagged leaves? Students begin with real plants and seeds, then investigate the tiny instructions behind those visible traits. They plant fast-growing seeds, track changes in a journal and watch colored water travel through celery stems. The class moves from plant parts into genetics. Students extract DNA from strawberries, build a double-helix model with paired bases and compare inherited traits with learned traits. They open soaked beans to find the embryo, seed coat and cotyledon, explore pollination and group plants into families by shared features. Each student invents a plant with its own DNA pattern, traits, habitat and helpful mutation. They develop the idea through capstone checkpoints, rehearse their explanation and present the finished model during a Plant Genetics Showcase. This three-week course is part of Summer Discovery’s Institute for the Gifted program on Bryn Mawr College’s campus in Bryn Mawr, Pennsylvania. The program is available to commuter students. Beyond class, students take part in campus activities, make new friends, and build confidence trying something new.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Plant fast-growing seeds and record changes in a plant journal • Watch colored water move through celery stems and compare the results • Extract visible strands of DNA from strawberries • Build a double-helix model using the A-T and C-G pairing patterns • Investigate seeds, inherited traits, habitats, pollination and plant mutations • Design and present an original plant with its own DNA, traits and habitat

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain how DNA carries instructions that influence plant traits • Observe plant growth and record evidence using drawings and simple descriptions • Create and present a model that connects DNA, traits, mutations and habitat Students will leave with a course completion certificate, a plant journal, a double-helix model and an original plant capstone that may spark more questions about genetics and the natural world.

Scientific ideas are introduced through concrete experiments, creative making, and age-appropriate explanations. View the eligibility requirements for the Institute for the Gifted on our FAQ page. A completed program application is required.

description_full: How can a collection of numbers reveal a pattern, test an idea, or help someone make a prediction? Students begin by asking where data science appears in everyday life, then set up Anaconda and Jupyter notebooks to explore Python syntax, variables, expressions, and different data types. Hands-on investigations make statistical thinking concrete. Students review mean, median, mode, and outliers through card-based activities, then use Pandas DataFrames to import, clean, slice, and analyze datasets. They practice removing missing values, isolating columns, creating bar graphs, pie charts, and histograms, and choosing labels and formats that make a visualization clear. As their skills grow, students examine correlation versus causation, consider how interpretation changes a data story, and explore introductory linear regression. Capstone checkpoints guide each student from selecting a dataset and question to building a documented Jupyter notebook with analysis, visualizations, and conclusions. The course concludes with student presentations that explain both the findings and the reasoning behind them. description_full: Which paper airplane flies farthest? Is there really more of one candy color in the bag? Students become data detectives, using numbers as clues to answer questions through games and hands-on experiments. They sort candies, measure rolling balls, compare basketball scores, and test their predictions with classmates. The discoveries take shape in colorful graphs and simple tables. Students explore averages, middle values, and numbers that appear most often, then notice how much results change from one try to the next. Dice and spinner games introduce chance. Class surveys show how asking a question differently can change someone’s answer, while weather observations reveal patterns over time. For their final detective project, students choose something they want to find out. They make a prediction, gather information, create graphs, and share what they discovered. The fun is in following the clues, finding surprises, and explaining the answer in their own words. This three-week course is part of Summer Discovery’s Institute for the Gifted program on Bryn Mawr College’s campus in Bryn Mawr, Pennsylvania. The course is available to commuter students. Beyond class, children make new friends, enjoy campus activities, and build confidence trying something new.

curriculum_sections.body: • Sort and count candy colors, then turn the results into a graph • Test paper airplanes and measure how far each design flies • Compare basketball scores and rolling-ball distances to spot patterns • Ask classmates survey questions and explore what makes a question fair • Roll dice and spin spinners to compare predictions with results • Choose a question, collect clues in the data, and share your discoveries

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Collect and organize results from a survey or hands-on experiment • Use graphs, averages, and number patterns to describe what they notice • Explain an answer to their own question using the information they collected Students will leave with their own data-detective project, graphs to share, new math and teamwork skills, and more questions they are excited to explore.

The focus is on joining in, trying things out, and learning from the results. Curiosity and a willingness to work together help students get the most from the activities. Please see the Institute for the Gifted eligibility requirements on our FAQ page.

description_full: Engineers turn needs into questions they can investigate. Students explore how civil, chemical, electrical, biomedical, and mechanical engineers approach different problems, then use the engineering design process to ask, imagine, plan, create, test, and improve. Hands-on challenges make core principles visible. Students investigate structural stability, buoyancy, heat, simple electrical systems, materials, and machines. They create blueprints, mix and test materials, build prototypes, measure performance, and compare how a change affects the result. Collaboration asks teams to explain tradeoffs instead of assuming there is one perfect design. For the capstone, students identify a challenge in their community or the wider world and engineer a response. They research the need, define criteria and constraints, develop and test a concept, and present the design process. Final work may include a prototype, blueprint, or multimedia model that shows how the proposed solution could improve life. description_full: A courtroom argument must connect a claim to evidence and explain why that evidence matters. Students practice that structure through the claim, warrant, data and impact model, then learn how voice, pacing, questioning and listening affect whether an argument is understood. A scripted Goldilocks trial introduces courtroom roles and procedure. Students write openings, develop a case theory, prepare direct and cross-examinations, practice objections and compare open-ended questions with leading questions. SPAR debates require teams to argue assigned positions and respond to critique, helping students test ideas before the final trial. The capstone turns the events of the book Holes into a child-labor case involving Camp Green Lake. Prosecution and defense teams research the text, organize admissible evidence, assign attorneys and witnesses, prepare questions and anticipate opposing claims. During the final mock trial, students deliver openings and closings, question witnesses, raise objections and perform their assigned courtroom roles. This three-week course is part of Summer Discovery’s Institute for the Gifted program on Bryn Mawr College’s campus in Bryn Mawr, Pennsylvania. The program is available to commuter students. Beyond class, students take part in campus activities, make new friends, and build confidence and independence in a college setting.

curriculum_sections.body: • Build arguments using claims, warrants, data and impacts • Practice vocal delivery, active listening and question-based speaking games • Perform a scripted Goldilocks trial to learn courtroom roles • Write openings, direct examinations, cross-examinations and objections • Present assigned positions in SPAR debates and respond to critique • Prepare and perform a child-labor mock trial based on Holes

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Construct an evidence-based argument with a clear claim and supporting reasoning • Use direct questions, leading questions and objections appropriately in a mock trial • Perform a courtroom role and respond to opposing arguments during a complete case Students will leave with a course completion certificate, written trial materials and experience performing two mock trials, plus a clearer sense of what they may want to explore next in law, debate or public speaking.

description_full: Microorganisms are everywhere, but their effects range from helpful to harmful. Students begin with the history of medical microbiology and the scientists whose discoveries changed how people understand infection. A Glo Germ investigation makes transmission visible and gives students evidence for testing a handwashing protocol. The course compares bacteria, viruses, fungi, and other microbes, then connects them to immune-system responses, infectious disease, microbiomes, and biotechnology. Students sort microbes by function, map immune cells involved in different disorders, research how a treatment affects a disease process, and communicate findings through diagrams and short presentations. For the capstone, students identify a challenge or opportunity where microorganisms play an important role. They investigate the underlying biology, current approaches, and emerging trends, then propose a scientifically grounded response. Checkpoints guide research, evidence, and presentation so the final project explains both the problem and the microbiological reasoning behind the solution. This three-week course is part of Summer Discovery’s Institute for the Gifted program on Bryn Mawr College’s campus in Bryn Mawr, Pennsylvania. The program is available to commuter students. Beyond class, students take part in campus activities, make new friends, and build confidence and independence in a college setting.

description_full: Choosing a stock is only the beginning. Students ask what makes a company worth investigating, how an investor’s goals shape strategy, and why return cannot be considered without risk, fees, and time. The course makes financial ideas visible through articles, videos, group analysis, and portfolio work. Students compare stock-picking criteria, use free screeners, examine company profiles and financial ratios, and build a hypothetical portfolio. As prices change, they calculate return on investment, review allocation choices, and consider how taxes, commissions, interest rates, and different risk profiles affect an outcome. The capstone brings those decisions into one investment presentation. Students document the companies and industries selected, explain their allocation, create a portfolio graphic, track performance, and defend the reasoning behind changes. Students compare results with classmates and revise their reasoning. The goal is not to predict the market. It is to practice making informed choices and explaining the evidence behind them. This three-week course is part of Summer Discovery’s Institute for the Gifted program on Bryn Mawr College’s campus in Bryn Mawr, Pennsylvania. The program is available to commuter students. Beyond class, students take part in campus activities, make new friends, and build confidence and independence in a college setting.

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Compare investments using goals, company information, risk, and financial ratios • Calculate portfolio value and return while accounting for common costs • Present and defend a researched portfolio strategy Students will leave with a tracked hypothetical portfolio and presentation, useful exposure to investing and finance, and a clearer sense of which money topics they want to explore next.

Short readings, oral retellings, and reader’s theater introduce age-appropriate myths, legends, and folktales from several cultural traditions. Students compare story patterns while paying attention to differences in setting, purpose, and cultural context. During the final week, each student creates an original myth-inspired story around a big question, natural phenomenon, or human value. Writing workshops, peer feedback, and rehearsal lead to an illustrated story, comic, script, or narrated audio piece presented at a Myth Makers Storytelling Festival. description_full: The ocean connects tiny plankton, enormous marine mammals, coastal communities, and the global climate. Students investigate life from coral reefs to the ocean floor while asking how organisms are adapted to water, food webs, temperature, depth, and one another. Experiments and research make ocean systems tangible. Students test density, model the water cycle, examine ocean chemistry, and compare evolutionary and ecological relationships among marine plants and animals. They research a chosen organism, communicate its adaptations, and consider how temperature change, pollution, fishing, habitat loss, or other human activity may affect it. For the capstone, students investigate a marine issue and its effects on local animals, plants, and people. They propose a solution designed to benefit both communities and the environment, then plan how it could gain funding, supplies, or public support. A mock-election presentation asks them to defend the evidence and practicality behind the proposal. This three-week course is part of Summer Discovery’s Institute for the Gifted program on Bryn Mawr College’s campus in Bryn Mawr, Pennsylvania. The program is available to commuter students. Beyond class, students take part in campus activities, make new friends, and build confidence trying something new.

description_full: What makes a machine a robot? Students compare familiar robots, investigate the jobs they perform, and identify the sensors, instructions, movement, and feedback that allow a robot to act. A human “robot and programmer” activity shows why precise commands matter before students move into block-based coding. Using Microsoft MakeCode and Finch robots, students create sequences, control motion, test lights and sound, and adjust programs after observing what the robot actually does. Challenges include drawing geometric paths, measuring movement, and using code to reproduce patterns. Students learn to break a larger goal into smaller steps and debug one variable at a time. The capstone combines programming and creative engineering. Students develop an interactive Finch performance or art challenge inspired by activities such as the bee waggle dance and Mondrian-style drawing. They plan the behavior, write and test the code, document revisions, and demonstrate how the robot responds to their instructions. This three-week course is part of Summer Discovery’s Institute for the Gifted program on Bryn Mawr College’s campus in Bryn Mawr, Pennsylvania. The program is available to commuter students. Next, the class moves outward. Students create a walkable solar-system model, compare rocky planets and giant worlds, test how impacts form craters, and design a rover or lander for the conditions on a chosen planet or moon. A light-and-orbit demonstration introduces how astronomers discover planets beyond our solar system. The final week brings stars, galaxies, and the scale of the universe into view through image sorting, sequencing, art, and nesting models. Teams create a Space Discovery Museum exhibit with a model or interactive visual, labeled explanation, surprising fact, and short presentation. description_full: How do the brain, body, and environment work together to shape attention, stress, perception, and behavior? Students build a foundation in neuroanatomy and neural function while exploring the emerging field of environmental neuroscience. Hands-on activities make the science tangible. Students use an interactive brain atlas, build and label a neuron, test perception and attention, practice breathing techniques, and examine how habits and circadian rhythms affect well-being. A guided walk in Pine Park turns attention restoration into a field observation, while a sheep brain lab connects models and anatomy. A visit to Dartmouth Hitchcock Medical Center introduces clinical and research settings connected with neurology, neuroimaging, psychiatry, or rehabilitation. In small groups, students then develop a research question and present a capstone project that connects neuroscience evidence with a topic they want to explore in greater depth. This two-week full-day academy is part of Dartmouth Precollege Summer Scholars. Students spend the full program focused on one intensive academy. The academy is available to residential students and will take place both on Dartmouth's main campus as well as the legendary mountain retreat, Moosilauke Ravine Lodge, where outdoor experiences become part of the learning and development. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed and academically led by Dartmouth.

Case studies, spreadsheets, financial analysis, and group discussions help students examine how companies identify customers, generate revenue, finance growth, compete, manage risk, and evaluate new opportunities. description_full: Students examine the technologies, policies, and ethical choices shaping the transition to a lower-carbon future. The course brings together climate science, engineering, economics, philosophy, medicine, and public policy so that energy decisions are considered from several angles. Students calculate personal carbon footprints, interpret emissions data, compare energy technologies, and debate climate policy. Case studies and collaborative projects ask them to connect individual choices with infrastructure, economics, air quality, environmental justice, and public action. A carbon-tax versus cap-and-trade simulation asks students to negotiate from the perspectives of governments, businesses, citizens, and nongovernmental organizations. Guest speakers and a visit to Dartmouth’s Bone Lab add perspectives from climate science, environmental anthropology, medicine, ecology, agriculture, and sustainability. Students are asked to distinguish a promising technology from a complete climate strategy. Their final project must address emissions, cost, feasibility, equity, policy, infrastructure, and human behavior in a realistic decarbonization plan for a community or system they know. This two-week full-day academy is part of Dartmouth Precollege Summer Scholars. Students spend the full program focused on one intensive academy. The academy is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed and academically led by Dartmouth.

description_full: Students study why international conflicts begin, how they end, and what diplomats and institutions can do when interests collide. Case studies and current events introduce civil war, peacekeeping, negotiation, and the role of the United Nations in international security. Research and simulation place students inside the problem. They evaluate sources, compare stakeholder positions, identify trade-offs, build coalitions, and draft resolutions. Library research and guest speakers from Dartmouth’s Dickey Center for International Understanding connect the work to international-affairs practice. The academy culminates in a United Nations Security Council simulation focused on conflicts in Sudan, the Democratic Republic of Congo, and Somalia. Representing member states, students prepare briefings, draft resolutions, negotiate agreements, and respond to questions while balancing their assigned country’s priorities. Preparation for the simulation is cumulative. Research defines each state's interests, drafted language makes proposals precise, and live negotiation reveals which goals are essential and where compromise is possible. The final crisis response tests all three at once. This two-week full-day academy is part of Dartmouth Precollege Summer Scholars. Students spend the full program focused on one intensive academy. description_full: Dartmouth’s outdoor spaces become both subject and classroom as students explore how place can shape voice, imagination, and memory. Guided walks, meditation, close observation, and daily writing exercises turn encounters with the natural world into material for original work. Students experiment with poetry, short fiction, and creative nonfiction. Readings and lessons in imagery, metaphor, voice, sensory detail, point of view, and narrative structure give them tools for developing drafts. Writing sessions in places such as Pine Park, Occum Pond, BEMA, and the Robert Frost site provide changing settings and perspectives. Collaborative workshops add the discipline of revision. Students share work, give constructive feedback, decide what to change, and assemble a small portfolio of revised pieces. A closing reading gives them the chance to present selected work to the class. The outdoor setting is used as a source of specific observation, not simply a backdrop. Students return to their notes and drafts throughout the academy, noticing how a change in form, detail, or point of view can reshape the same experience. This two-week full-day academy is part of Dartmouth Precollege Summer Scholars. Students spend the full program focused on one intensive academy. The academy is available to residential students and will take place both on Dartmouth's main campus as well as the legendary mountain retreat, Moosilauke Ravine Lodge, where outdoor experiences become part of the learning and development. description_full: Students experience engineering as a cycle of defining a problem, building a possible solution, testing it, and using evidence to improve the design. Challenges require attention to user needs, feasibility, durability, efficiency, sustainability, safety, and cost rather than a single ideal answer. Teams spend at least 40% of the academy building and testing. They compare materials through stiffness, impact, friction, and wear tests; create two prototype versions; collect measurements; identify failure modes; and use the evidence to decide what to change. Entrepreneurship is integrated throughout the process. Students define a value proposition, estimate cost of goods sold, compare alternatives, consider manufacturing and lifecycle impacts, and explain why a design is worth pursuing. A technical dossier, poster, slide deck, live demonstration, and founder-style pitch document the finished work. Each testing cycle creates a record of engineering judgment. Students compare what they expected with what happened, identify the most important failure or constraint, and use that evidence to decide which change is most likely to improve the next version. This two-week full-day academy is part of Dartmouth Precollege Summer Scholars. Students spend the full program focused on one intensive academy. The academy is available to residential and commuter students. curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Create and refine a functional prototype through evidence-based build-test-learn cycles • Use material tests, performance data, and failure analysis to justify design decisions • Communicate a solution through a technical dossier, poster, live demonstration, and founder-style pitch Students leave with two prototype versions and several portfolio-ready artifacts, stronger technical problem-solving skills, and clearer direction about engineering, product design, materials, manufacturing, or entrepreneurship.

Topics include preventative medicine, nutrition, epidemiology, public health, diagnostic reasoning, emergency medicine, trauma care, and patient communication. description_full: Students follow the path from basic scientific discovery to clinical application. Hands-on laboratory work, interactive seminars, and visits to Dartmouth research settings introduce the methods and institutions that help move an idea from the laboratory bench to patient care. Students practice microscopy and micropipetting, examine cell division, diagnose a sickle cell case through gel electrophoresis, test enzyme activity in a catalase lab, and compare brain structures in a preserved sheep brain dissection. A zebrafish lab visit introduces model organisms and confocal microscopy. Two visits to Dartmouth Hitchcock Medical Center extend the investigation into chemistry and microbiology labs, pathology, clinical simulation, genomics, and medical imaging. Students also examine clinical trials, regulation, research ethics, and the responsibilities involved in human and animal research. In teams of two or three, students choose a cutting-edge medical topic, find both primary and reputable secondary sources, and create a visual and oral presentation. The project asks them to explain the most important findings clearly and connect the topic with the bench-to-bedside process. This two-week full-day academy is part of Dartmouth Precollege Summer Scholars. Students spend the full program focused on one intensive academy. The academy is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed and academically led by Dartmouth.

description_full: How do you make a convincing point when every word, response, and cultural cue matters? Students strengthen spoken Spanish through the Rassias Method, which uses dramatic techniques, rhythmic drills, rapid reinforcement, and an error-tolerant classroom to encourage natural speech. Lead classes, reinforcement sessions, group lunches in Spanish, cultural programming, debates, negotiations, and presentations place grammar and vocabulary inside active communication. Students practice forming arguments, responding to counterarguments, and adapting persuasive choices to Spanish-speaking contexts. The emphasis stays on oral comprehension and spontaneous speech. Because the method depends on frequent participation, students keep returning to the language under different conditions. A phrase first practiced in a drill may reappear in a discussion, negotiation, cultural session, or unscripted response. The academy builds toward an approximately 15-minute verbal presentation on a topic each student has studied or cares about, followed by questions and answers. Students must organize an argument, speak with clarity, and respond in the moment. This two-week, full-day intensive academy is part of Dartmouth Precollege Summer Scholars in Hanover, New Hampshire. The academy is fully developed and run by Dartmouth and taught by Dartmouth faculty and expert instructors. Residential and commuter students participate throughout the day, pairing focused academic work with campus life and growing independence.

description_full: Leadership is often treated as a title. Dartmouth’s signature Leadership Institute treats it as a practice: understand yourself, earn trust, make decisions under uncertainty, and help a team move forward. Students begin on Dartmouth campus with leadership models, neuroscience, self-assessments, values work, case examples, and guided discussion that reveal how strengths, habits, and choices shape a group. They then practice communication, teamwork, resilience, and judgment through collaborative challenges and write a personal This I Believe leadership essay. During the second week, the classroom expands to Dartmouth’s Moosilauke Ravine Lodge, a setting connected to generations of Dartmouth students. Hiking, orienteering, team initiatives, trail work, and increasingly complex outdoor challenges make leadership visible: students must decide when to step forward, when to listen, how to adapt, and how to support others. Reflection after each experience turns action into a personal framework for continued growth. That combination of intensive study, place-based challenge, and reflection is unique within the Dartmouth Precollege Summer Scholars portfolio. Students leave with real examples of leadership—not simply a claim that they are leaders—that they can draw on in college essays, interviews, internship materials, and early job applications. In feedback from students who took the course, 98% said they would use the program in their college applications, and 93% said they would recommend it to a friend. This is a two-week, full-day academy. The academy is available to residential students and will take place both on Dartmouth's main campus as well as the legendary mountain retreat, Moosilauke Ravine Lodge, where outdoor experiences become part of the learning and development. Fully developed and run by Dartmouth, it is taught by Dartmouth faculty and expert instructors.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Explore leadership models, personal values, and real-world examples of decision making • Identify your strengths, habits, and growth priorities through self-assessment programs • Build communication, teamwork, resilience, and decision-making through group challenges • Define and develop your emerging leadership philosophy in a This I Believe essay • Expand the classroom at Moosilauke lodge—a Dartmouth tradition for generations—through hiking, navigation and team challenges • Translate feedback into personal leadership strengths and development priorities • Leave with a personalized growth framework with evidence, goals, and next steps

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Articulate a personal leadership philosophy grounded in values, leadership concepts, and reflection • Apply communication, collaboration, and decision-making strategies in classroom and outdoor challenges • Use a leadership essay and personal growth framework to demonstrate evidence of personal growth Students leave with a finished This I Believe essay, a personal leadership framework, and concrete experiences they can draw on in college, internship, and early job applications or interviews.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This academy is for motivated high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade, whether they already lead clubs and teams or are only beginning to see themselves as leaders. It is a strong fit across public policy, business, medicine, engineering, environmental studies, the arts, and community advocacy because every field depends on communication, judgment, and collaboration. No prior formal leadership experience is required. Students should be ready to participate fully in outdoor activities including hiking, orienteering and trail work. They should be ready to engage in group initiatives, personal writing, guided reflection, and constructive feedback. The experience rewards curiosity, self-awareness, resilience, and a willingness to contribute when conditions change.

description_full: Students investigate how genetic variation contributes to inherited disorders, complex disease, and differences in treatment. Case studies and current scientific literature provide a path into inheritance patterns, gene-environment interactions, genomics, and genetic testing. The course connects biological mechanisms with the growing field of precision medicine. Students examine how genomic information can support prevention, diagnosis, and treatment, then read primary research to determine what a study found and what remains uncertain. Scientific progress also raises social and ethical questions. Discussions of benefits, risks, privacy, access, and the effects of genetic knowledge ask students to consider how rapidly advancing technologies should be used. A visit to the Genomics Shared Resource Lab and a guest research perspective connect the work to current practice. The academy asks students to move carefully between a genetic association, a biological explanation, and a possible medical use. That distinction helps them recognize both the potential of genomics and the uncertainty that must accompany responsible interpretation. This two-week, full-day intensive academy is part of Dartmouth Precollege Summer Scholars in Hanover, New Hampshire. The academy is fully developed and run by Dartmouth and taught by Dartmouth faculty and expert instructors. Residential and commuter students participate throughout the day, pairing focused academic work with campus life and growing independence.

curriculum_sections.body: • Analyze inheritance patterns associated with genetic disease • Study gene-environment interactions and complex traits • Read and interpret primary research in human genetics • Examine genomics, genetic testing, and precision medicine • Discuss the benefits, risks, and social implications of genetic research • Visit the Genomics Shared Resource Lab • Present an evidence-based explanation of a genetics question

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain inheritance patterns and gene-environment interactions in human disease • Interpret primary genetics research and connect genomic information with precision medicine • Evaluate scientific, ethical, and social implications of genetic testing and research Students leave with a research-based genetics analysis, stronger scientific literacy, and clearer direction about biology, medicine, biotechnology, public health, or bioethics.

It is a strong fit for students who want to connect molecular mechanisms with patient and societal consequences. Participants should be ready to read scientific material, analyze inheritance patterns, discuss uncertainty, and engage respectfully with sensitive questions about genetic information. The source does not list a formal prerequisite. Prior biology may be helpful, but careful reading and curiosity are the main expectations.

description_full: What contributes to lasting well-being, and which popular ideas about happiness hold up under scientific study? Students examine happiness, resilience, and human flourishing through positive psychology, neuroscience, sociology, and behavioral science. Research discussions, reflective journaling, and experiential activities introduce gratitude, purpose, motivation, relationships, mindfulness, emotional intelligence, optimism, and resilience. Students evaluate evidence, question common misconceptions, and consider how individual habits and social conditions can influence well-being. As students move between research and reflection, they consider where evidence is persuasive, where questions remain open, and why a practice may not affect every person in the same way. Personal experience becomes something to examine, not universal proof. The academy connects scientific analysis with thoughtful reflection. Students test evidence-based practices, examine their own values and goals, and communicate psychological concepts without turning one strategy into a universal prescription. This two-week, full-day intensive academy is part of Dartmouth Precollege Summer Scholars in Hanover, New Hampshire. The academy is fully developed and run by Dartmouth and taught by Dartmouth faculty and expert instructors. The broader experience connects focused academic exploration with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study next.

description_full: How can an object reveal the life of a person who used it long ago? Students practice the archaeologist’s core move: observing carefully before making an inference. Mystery bags, artifact descriptions, and replica-making challenges show how shape, material, context, and missing information affect an interpretation. Hands-on investigations include creating clay vessels or figurines, designing hieroglyphic stories, mapping a familiar or imagined place with symbols, and testing tool shapes through a bird-beak experiment. Students compare evidence, record what they notice, and explain why one conclusion is better supported than another. Activities also explore how early people solved problems with available natural materials. For the capstone, students select an archaeological question or site concept and assemble evidence into a poster, map, model, or exhibit-style presentation. They label observations and inferences separately, explain the limits of the evidence, and share what additional information would strengthen their conclusion. This three-week course is part of Summer Discovery’s Institute for the Gifted program on Fairfield University’s campus. The course is available to commuter students. Beyond class, students connect engaging academic exploration with campus life, new friendships, growing confidence, and curiosity about what students may want to explore next.

curriculum_sections.body: • Separate observations from inferences when examining artifacts • Reconstruct an object from a limited archaeological description • Create symbols and a hieroglyphic story • Map a site using scale, landmarks, and a clear legend • Test how tool shapes affect performance through an experiment • Design and present an evidence-based archaeology capstone

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Use artifact features and context to make a supported inference about the past • Create maps, models, and records that document archaeological evidence • Present an interpretation while explaining uncertainty and missing information Students will leave with replica artifacts, field-style records, and a capstone display showing how evidence can be used to reconstruct part of the human past.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for elementary school students who have completed 4th or 5th grade and enjoy history, mysteries, maps, making objects, or asking how we know what happened long ago. It fits careful observers who like combining clues and explaining their reasoning. Students should be ready to handle materials responsibly, record details, work with classmates, and revise an interpretation when new evidence appears. A strong participant brings curiosity, patience, and a willingness to revise. The most important preparation is readiness to ask questions and take part.

description_full: Children are already experts at asking why. Big Questions Club gives that curiosity a place to grow through stories, puzzles, mystery objects, movement, drawing, and role-play. As students explore questions about fairness, friendship, rules, and how we know what is true, they learn to explain what they think, listen to different ideas, and discover how a thoughtful question can lead somewhere unexpected. Each day turns one big idea into something students can see and do. Students might act out ways to share materials, follow instructions like a paper robot, sort clues to decide what can be known, or build a gallery around what makes something beautiful. They can participate through speaking, drawing, acting, or building. In the final week, each student chooses a favorite question and creates a Big Questions Gallery project. A poster, comic, model, or interactive display presents two possible answers, the student’s current view, and the reasons behind it. Students also complete an illustrated philosophy journal and share their finished work. This three-week course is part of Summer Discovery’s Institute for the Gifted program on Fairfield University’s campus. It is available to commuter students. Beyond class, students connect hands-on learning with campus life, new friendships, and growing confidence.

description_full: Why does a plant have tall stems, purple flowers or jagged leaves? Students begin with real plants and seeds, then investigate the tiny instructions behind those visible traits. They plant fast-growing seeds, track changes in a journal and watch colored water travel through celery stems. The class moves from plant parts into genetics. Students extract DNA from strawberries, build a double-helix model with paired bases and compare inherited traits with learned traits. They open soaked beans to find the embryo, seed coat and cotyledon, explore pollination and group plants into families by shared features. Each student invents a plant with its own DNA pattern, traits, habitat and helpful mutation. They develop the idea through capstone checkpoints, rehearse their explanation and present the finished model during a Plant Genetics Showcase. This three-week course is part of Summer Discovery’s Institute for the Gifted program on Fairfield University’s campus. The course is available to commuter students. Beyond class, students connect engaging academic exploration with a welcoming campus community, growing confidence, and curiosity students can carry into what they explore next.

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain how DNA carries instructions that influence plant traits • Observe plant growth and record evidence using drawings and simple descriptions • Create and present a model that connects DNA, traits, mutations and habitat Students will leave with a course completion certificate, a plant journal, a double-helix model and an original plant capstone that may spark more questions about genetics and the natural world.

description_full: Which paper airplane flies farthest? Is there really more of one candy color in the bag? Students become data detectives, using numbers as clues to answer questions through games and hands-on experiments. They sort candies, measure rolling balls, compare basketball scores, and test their predictions with classmates. The discoveries take shape in colorful graphs and simple tables. Students explore averages, middle values, and numbers that appear most often, then notice how much results change from one try to the next. Dice and spinner games introduce chance. Class surveys show how asking a question differently can change someone’s answer, while weather observations reveal patterns over time. For their final detective project, students choose something they want to find out. They make a prediction, gather information, create graphs, and share what they discovered. The fun is in following the clues, finding surprises, and explaining the answer in their own words. This three-week course is part of Summer Discovery’s Institute for the Gifted program on Fairfield University’s campus in Fairfield, Connecticut. The course is available to commuter students. Beyond class, children make new friends, enjoy campus activities, and build confidence trying something new.

curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Collect and organize results from a survey or hands-on experiment • Use graphs, averages, and number patterns to describe what they notice • Explain an answer to their own question using the information they collected Students will leave with their own data-detective project, graphs to share, new math and teamwork skills, and more questions they are excited to explore.

Please see the Institute for the Gifted eligibility requirements on our FAQ page.

Students explore how civil, chemical, electrical, biomedical, and mechanical engineers approach different problems, then use the engineering design process to ask, imagine, plan, create, test, and improve. Hands-on challenges make core principles visible. Students investigate structural stability, buoyancy, heat, simple electrical systems, materials, and machines. They create blueprints, mix and test materials, build prototypes, measure performance, and compare how a change affects the result. Collaboration asks teams to explain tradeoffs instead of assuming there is one perfect design. For the capstone, students identify a challenge in their community or the wider world and engineer a response. They research the need, define criteria and constraints, develop and test a concept, and present the design process. Final work may include a prototype, blueprint, or multimedia model that shows how the proposed solution could improve life. Students learn how persuasive speakers organize an argument, connect ideas with reasons, and prepare a speech that others can follow. Practice turns those ideas into communication. description_full: The ocean connects tiny plankton, enormous marine mammals, coastal communities, and the global climate. Students investigate life from coral reefs to the ocean floor while asking how organisms are adapted to water, food webs, temperature, depth, and one another. Experiments and research make ocean systems tangible. Students test density, model the water cycle, examine ocean chemistry, and compare evolutionary and ecological relationships among marine plants and animals. They research a chosen organism, communicate its adaptations, and consider how temperature change, pollution, fishing, habitat loss, or other human activity may affect it. For the capstone, students investigate a marine issue and its effects on local animals, plants, and people. They propose a solution designed to benefit both communities and the environment, then plan how it could gain funding, supplies, or public support. A mock-election presentation asks them to defend the evidence and practicality behind the proposal. Students compare familiar robots, investigate the jobs they perform, and identify the sensors, instructions, movement, and feedback that allow a robot to act. A human “robot and programmer” activity shows why precise commands matter before students move into block-based coding. description_full: Every memorable story begins with a character who wants something. Students explore how traits, motivations, settings, problems, and solutions work together. They invent characters from everyday materials, compare familiar archetypes, and use puppets or models to discover how a character’s design can suggest movement, personality, and story choices. Creative engineering adds a second challenge: a model must stand, move, or communicate an idea. Students sketch, build, test, and improve three-dimensional characters and story elements. Mind maps, sequencing activities, and oral storytelling help them connect the physical design to a beginning, middle, and end. For the capstone, each student creates an original superhero story and a 3D model that represents the central character or invention. Checkpoints guide topic choice, character development, plot, construction, and rehearsal. Students present the finished story, demonstrate the model, and explain how design decisions support the character and narrative. This three-week course is part of Summer Discovery’s Institute for the Gifted program on Fairfield University’s campus. The course is available to commuter students. Beyond class, students connect engaging academic exploration with a welcoming campus community, growing confidence, and curiosity students can carry into what they explore next.

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes

Students should be ready to use age-appropriate craft materials, listen to classmates’ stories, try more than one design, and speak during a supportive final sharing. subject: Engineering

description_full: A toothpick tower must stand tall without toppling. A pizza-box oven must capture enough heat to work. Students tackle playful challenges like these by taking objects apart, putting them together, and thinking with their hands. Along the way, they use ideas from science, engineering, math, and art to plan and create original designs. Students investigate ancient and modern engineering wonders and explore how chemical, civil, electrical, and mechanical engineers solve different problems. Geometry helps them plan structures, while experiments with heat, materials, and physical forces show how a design behaves. Each challenge gives students a chance to build, test, notice what happened, and try again. For the capstone, students choose a real-world concern connected to one of the engineering branches they explored. They design a solution as a model, prototype, detailed blueprint, or original product, then explain their engineering choices to classmates. This three-week course is part of Summer Discovery’s Institute for the Gifted program on Fairfield University’s campus in Fairfield, Connecticut. The program is available to commuter students. Beyond class, students take part in campus activities, make new friends, and build confidence trying something new.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Take apart and reassemble objects to investigate how they work • Explore ancient and modern engineering wonders • Use geometry to design and build a toothpick tower • Apply heat-energy concepts while creating a pizza-box oven • Compare chemical, civil, electrical, and mechanical engineering • Design and present a solution to a real-world concern

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Apply a build-test-improve process to an engineering challenge • Explain how geometry, heat, materials, or physical forces affect a design • Present a model, prototype, blueprint, or product that addresses a real-world concern Students will leave with hands-on challenge work and an original capstone solution that reflects new engineering skills and curiosity to keep creating.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for elementary school students who have completed 1st, 2nd, or 3rd grade and enjoy building, taking things apart, drawing plans, experimenting, or asking how everyday objects work. It is a good fit for curious makers who want to try several kinds of engineering through hands-on challenges. No prerequisites are required. Students should be ready to share materials, work with classmates, follow instructions for classroom tools, and keep trying when a design needs improvement. Students must bring a laptop or compatible tablet, a charger, and compatible headphones. View the eligibility requirements for the Institute for the Gifted on our FAQ page.

learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Apply a build-test-improve process to an engineering challenge • Explain how geometry, heat, materials, or physical forces affect a design • Present a model, prototype, blueprint, or product that addresses a real-world concern Students will leave with hands-on challenge work and an original capstone solution that reflects new engineering skills and curiosity to keep creating.

title: Advanced Debate: Persuasive Public Speaking
subject: Humanities
price_note: The course detail page does not publish a course-specific tuition; campus-level range retained.
description_short: What makes an argument persuasive when the stakes are high? Students examine how structure, evidence, word choice, voice, pacing, and body language influence an audience. Short speaking games and low-pressure speeches give them repeated opportunities to organize ideas, test delivery choices, and respond to focused feedback. The course moves from individual s
description_full: What makes an argument persuasive when the stakes are high? Students examine how structure, evidence, word choice, voice, pacing, and body language influence an audience. Short speaking games and low-pressure speeches give them repeated opportunities to organize ideas, test delivery choices, and respond to focused feedback. The course moves from individual speaking to structured argument. Students develop claims, reasons, evidence, counterarguments, and rebuttals, then practice cross-examination and respectful questioning. Argument maps help teams see where a position is strong, where evidence is missing, and how an opposing side may respond. Students also learn how judges evaluate clarity, logic, listening, and fairness. A final team debate brings the process together. Students prepare roles, research support, draft questions and closing statements, complete practice rounds, and revise before presenting. Every student contributes as a speaker, debater, or judge, applying persuasive communication while listening carefully and disagreeing with respect. This two-week course takes place at Georgetown University. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by Georgetown University and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Organize short speeches with clear openings, evidence, and conclusions • Practice posture, eye contact, pacing, tone, and audience awareness • Build argument maps from claims, reasons, and supporting evidence • Develop respectful rebuttals and cross-examination questions • Apply a scoring template while serving as a debate judge • Prepare and participate in a structured final team debate

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Organize and deliver a persuasive speech for a defined audience • Construct and defend an evidence-based argument while addressing counterclaims • Evaluate a debate using criteria for clarity, evidence, refutation, and listening Students leave with practiced speeches, debate materials, and a stronger ability to communicate with clarity and purpose.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and want to become more persuasive speakers, thoughtful listeners, and strategic participants in discussion. It fits interests in debate, law, government, business, leadership, journalism, or any field that values clear communication. Participants should be willing to speak in front of classmates, research an issue, collaborate with a team, and give and receive respectful feedback. No formal debate experience is required. Students who are ready to practice, revise, and engage with opposing views will benefit most.

learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Organize and deliver a persuasive speech for a defined audience • Construct and defend an evidence-based argument while addressing counterclaims • Evaluate a debate using criteria for clarity, evidence, refutation, and listening Students leave with practiced speeches, debate materials, and a stronger ability to communicate with clarity and purpose.

title: Advertising: Consumer Behavior & Campaign Strategy
subject: Business, Leadership & Entrepreneurship
price_note: The course detail page does not publish a course-specific tuition; campus-level range retained.
description_short: Why does one advertisement connect while another gets ignored? Students explore advertising, marketing communications, and public relations across print, magazines, radio, television, social media, direct mail, and out-of-home media. They examine what a brand represents and how channel, message, and audience work together. Each class pairs concepts with a cr
description_full: Why does one advertisement connect while another gets ignored? Students explore advertising, marketing communications, and public relations across print, magazines, radio, television, social media, direct mail, and out-of-home media. They examine what a brand represents and how channel, message, and audience work together. Each class pairs concepts with a creative challenge. Teams respond to a brief by developing an advertisement in the medium under study, then explain how their idea fits the audience and objective. Discussions of challenger brands, celebrity endorsements, campaigns, and public relations show how communication choices can build attention, shape perception, or create risk. Quizzes reinforce vocabulary and strategy from previous sessions, while repeated team work builds speed and confidence. By comparing formats and creating across channels, students learn that an effective campaign requires more than a clever line. It needs a clear purpose, a specific audience, and execution suited to the way people encounter the message. This two-week course takes place at Georgetown University. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by Georgetown University and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Define advertising, marketing communications, public relations, and brand strategy • Interpret a creative brief for a specific audience and objective • Develop print and magazine advertising concepts in teams • Adapt messages for direct mail and out-of-home formats • Create ideas for radio, television, and social media • Present creative choices and respond to peer feedback

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain how audience, objective, brand, and medium shape an advertisement • Develop an advertising concept that responds to a creative brief • Compare communication formats and justify channel-specific creative choices Students leave with a set of cross-channel advertising concepts and a stronger foundation in strategic communications.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and are interested in advertising, brands, media, storytelling, consumer behavior, or public relations. It suits students who want to pair creative ideas with the strategy behind why a message works. Participants should be ready to discuss examples, work in teams, respond to briefs, present concepts, and learn through frequent quizzes and creative challenges. No specialized design software or prior advertising coursework is required. Curiosity about media and willingness to explain creative choices are strong indicators of fit.

subject: Business, Leadership & Entrepreneurship
price_note: The course detail page does not publish a course-specific tuition; campus-level range retained.
description_short: What turns an idea into a business people can understand and support? Students examine the qualities of entrepreneurs, debate whether successful founders are born or made, and study the origin stories behind startups and iconic brands. Each discussion leads into a learning lab where they test the concept for themselves. Students create a graphic startup blue
description_full: What turns an idea into a business people can understand and support? Students examine the qualities of entrepreneurs, debate whether successful founders are born or made, and study the origin stories behind startups and iconic brands. Each discussion leads into a learning lab where they test the concept for themselves. Students create a graphic startup blueprint, use art and music to shape a business vision, and evaluate case studies about measured risk. They build a rubric for future risk decisions, explore failure and resiliency through a game, and create visual media for a dream startup using software tools. A course audio-podcast activity and final business presentation give them practice organizing ideas for an audience. The work develops a practical view of entrepreneurship without asking students to have their future figured out. They learn to explain a vision, consider evidence, respond to questions, and see how passion, innovation, risk, and resilience affect a startup. This two-week course takes place at Georgetown University. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect active academic exploration with campus life, growing independence, new friendships, and a clearer sense of what students may want to explore next. The program is developed by Georgetown University and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Debate whether successful entrepreneurs are born or made • Research and record a startup founder for a course audio podcast • Create a graphic blueprint showing how a startup works • Shape and articulate a business vision through art and music • Evaluate risk cases and build a decision-making rubric • Create visual media and present a dream startup idea

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain how vision, innovation, risk, and resilience influence a startup • Evaluate an entrepreneurial decision using evidence and a risk rubric • Organize and present a clear business idea for an audience Students will leave with a startup blueprint, visual media, and a business presentation, plus a clearer sense of which parts of entrepreneurship they may want to explore next.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for middle school students who have completed 6th, 7th, or 8th grade and are curious about how ideas become businesses. It fits students who enjoy creative problem solving, brand stories, group challenges, or imagining a product, service, or organization they might build. Participants should be ready to discuss different viewpoints, complete individual and small-group learning labs, and present their thinking. The course balances creativity with practical decisions, so it can appeal to students drawn to design and storytelling as well as those interested in business, leadership, marketing, or finance.

subject: Business, Leadership & Entrepreneurship

description_short: What turns an interesting idea into a venture worth pursuing? Students enter a fast-moving startup studio and begin with opportunity recognition. In small teams, they identify a real problem, define the customer affected by it, and refine a concept through research, discussion, and feedback. The venture takes shape through the five Ps of business: product, p
description_full: What turns an interesting idea into a venture worth pursuing? Students enter a fast-moving startup studio and begin with opportunity recognition. In small teams, they identify a real problem, define the customer affected by it, and refine a concept through research, discussion, and feedback. The venture takes shape through the five Ps of business: product, price, promotion, place, and people. Students create a value proposition and logo, practice a speed pitch, explore marketing and sales, and consider how relationships, negotiation, culture, and international markets can affect execution. A simple financial snapshot asks teams to estimate startup costs, pricing, revenue, and feasibility. Teams also compare basic legal and business structures before preparing a one-page business summary and pitch deck. Each student speaks during the final presentation, explaining the problem, customer, solution, business logic, and changes made after feedback. The result is a practical introduction to iteration, teamwork, and the discipline behind entrepreneurial storytelling. This two-week course takes place at Georgetown University. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by Georgetown University and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Identify a customer problem or market opportunity • Develop a value proposition and refine a business concept • Map product, price, promotion, place, and people • Create a logo, speed pitch, and one-page business summary • Estimate startup costs, pricing, revenue, and feasibility • Build and deliver a collaborative investor-style pitch

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Define a customer problem and develop a focused value proposition • Evaluate a venture using marketing, financial, and organizational considerations • Present and defend a refined business concept with a team Students leave with a pitch deck, business one-pager, financial snapshot, and experience turning feedback into a stronger venture.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and want to build ideas, solve problems, or understand how startups move from concept to pitch. It fits interests in entrepreneurship, business, design, technology, marketing, finance, or social innovation. Participants should be ready to collaborate intensively, make assumptions visible, use basic spreadsheets and presentation tools, and speak during a final pitch. Students who are comfortable testing an idea, hearing feedback, and revising quickly will gain the most.

description_full: What turns an interesting idea into a venture worth pursuing? Students enter a fast-moving startup studio and begin with opportunity recognition. In small teams, they identify a real problem, define the customer affected by it, and refine a concept through research, discussion, and feedback. The venture takes shape through the five Ps of business: product, price, promotion, place, and people. Students create a value proposition and logo, practice a speed pitch, explore marketing and sales, and consider how relationships, negotiation, culture, and international markets can affect execution. A simple financial snapshot asks teams to estimate startup costs, pricing, revenue, and feasibility. Teams also compare basic legal and business structures before preparing a one-page business summary and pitch deck. Each student speaks during the final presentation, explaining the problem, customer, solution, business logic, and changes made after feedback. The result is a practical introduction to iteration, teamwork, and the discipline behind entrepreneurial storytelling. This two-week course takes place at Georgetown University. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by Georgetown University and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.
