description_full: How does the American legal system turn broad principles into decisions? Students examine the rule of law, justice, the Constitution, and the roles of the legislative, executive, and judicial branches. Landmark cases and current legal issues help them see how statutes, regulations, precedent, and constitutional rights shape everyday life. The course treats law as a practice, not only a body of facts. Students learn to brief a case by identifying the issue, relevant facts, reasoning, and decision. Small-group activities ask them to argue constitutional questions, compare civil and criminal matters, and follow a case through pleading, discovery, pretrial, trial, and post-trial stages. Legal vocabulary becomes useful through advocacy exercises. Students practice research, negotiation, cross-examination, and simulated trial work while considering the responsibilities of different legal professionals. Discussion emphasizes precise reasoning, supportable claims, and the ability to understand more than one side of a dispute. Discussion, practice, and feedback help students check their reasoning and improve how they communicate the work. This two-week course takes place at Georgetown University. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by Georgetown University and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Map the three branches of government and their legal roles • Analyze constitutional rights through a structured amendment argument • Brief a case by identifying issue, facts, reasoning, and decision • Compare civil and criminal cases and sources of law • Trace pleading, discovery, trial, and post-trial procedure • Practice negotiation, questioning, and simulated legal advocacy

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain core structures and sources within the American legal system • Brief a legal case and analyze competing arguments • Apply legal reasoning and advocacy skills in a simulated proceeding Students leave with case briefs, advocacy practice, and a clearer understanding of legal careers and the reasoning behind legal decisions.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and are interested in law, government, justice, policy, debate, or legal careers. It fits students who enjoy close reading, structured argument, and examining how rules apply to complicated facts. Participants should be ready to discuss contested issues respectfully, read cases, collaborate, and speak during simulations. Students who are willing to revise an argument when the facts or governing rule change will be especially well suited.

learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain core structures and sources within the American legal system • Brief a legal case and analyze competing arguments • Apply legal reasoning and advocacy skills in a simulated proceeding Students leave with case briefs, advocacy practice, and a clearer understanding of legal careers and the reasoning behind legal decisions.

subject: Medicine & Health Sciences
price_note: The course detail page does not publish a course-specific tuition; campus-level range retained.
description_short: Healthcare is a system of interconnected professions, not a single career track. Students compare clinical roles such as physicians, physician associates, nurses, and dentists with research, administration, policy, pharmaceutical, and health-technology pathways. For each, they examine daily responsibilities, working relationships, qualifications, and long-te
description_full: Healthcare is a system of interconnected professions, not a single career track. Students compare clinical roles such as physicians, physician associates, nurses, and dentists with research, administration, policy, pharmaceutical, and health-technology pathways. For each, they examine daily responsibilities, working relationships, qualifications, and long-term career outlook. The course follows the training behind the title. Students trace undergraduate, graduate, and professional steps, then consider how research advances medicine and how administrators and policy professionals shape care at scale. Discussions, projects, possible guest lectures, and videos connect formal pathways with the choices students can begin making in high school and college. Each student develops a personal career pathway project. Guided planning asks them to identify a profession of interest, relevant majors, education and training, volunteering or internship possibilities, and the strengths they want to build. A capstone presentation turns that research into a realistic next-step plan rather than a premature commitment. This two-week course takes place at Georgetown University. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by Georgetown University and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Map the healthcare ecosystem and compare professional roles • Trace education and training for physicians, nurses, and physician associates • Explore dentistry, biomedical research, administration, policy, and health technology • Compare daily responsibilities and long-term career outlooks • Research majors, volunteering, internships, and preparation options • Create and present a personal healthcare career pathway

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Compare clinical, research, and administrative healthcare careers • Explain the education, qualifications, and responsibilities of a selected profession • Develop a researched personal action plan for continued healthcare exploration Students leave with a completed career pathway project and clearer next steps for exploring the diverse world of healthcare.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and are considering medicine or want to understand the wider healthcare industry before choosing a direction. It fits interests in patient care, research, nursing, dentistry, policy, administration, pharmaceuticals, or health technology. Participants should be ready to research training pathways, ask questions, compare options, and reflect on their own interests and strengths. No clinical experience is required. Students who want an informed view of healthcare careers, including paths beyond becoming a physician, will benefit most.

learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Compare clinical, research, and administrative healthcare careers • Explain the education, qualifications, and responsibilities of a selected profession • Develop a researched personal action plan for continued healthcare exploration Students leave with a completed career pathway project and clearer next steps for exploring the diverse world of healthcare.

subject: Humanities
price_note: The course detail page does not publish a course-specific tuition; campus-level range retained.
description_short: What makes a college essay memorable when admissions readers already know a student’s grades and activities? Guided brainstorming helps them identify meaningful moments, mentors, challenges, identities, and experiences worth developing into an
description_full: What makes a college essay memorable when admissions readers already know a student’s grades and activities? Students learn how personal statements and supplemental essays can reveal character, perspective, growth, and goals. Guided brainstorming helps them identify meaningful moments, mentors, challenges, identities, and experiences worth developing into an authentic story. The workshop moves from idea generation to deliberate craft. Students practice showing instead of telling, add sensory detail, adapt ideas to different prompts, and organize an essay with a clear structure. Sample essays, hook activities, outlines, scene writing, and peer read-alouds help them test openings, strengthen reflection, and make their voice sound natural rather than generic. Revision turns an early draft into a focused application essay. Students examine tone, sentence flow, verb tense, punctuation, fragments, run-ons, and other mechanics that affect clarity. Peer review, “So What?” checks, grammar activities, self-editing, and a final checklist help them refine meaning as well as correctness. By the end, each student completes a polished draft that stays within expected limits and represents their own experience. This two-week course takes place at Georgetown University. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by Georgetown University and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Brainstorm personal experiences that could become compelling essay topics • Analyze personal statement and supplemental essay prompts • Practice sensory detail, scene writing, and showing instead of telling • Build an essay blueprint with a focused structure and opening hook • Give and apply peer feedback on voice, reflection, and clarity • Revise and proofread a college application essay using a final checklist

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Select and develop an authentic personal story for a college application prompt • Organize a focused essay using narrative structure, voice, and meaningful reflection • Revise a draft for clarity, coherence, grammar, mechanics, and required limits Students leave with a revised college application essay draft, stronger writing and feedback skills, and clearer direction for future academic and application writing.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and want structured support developing a college application essay. It fits students who have stories or experiences to share but need help choosing a topic, organizing the narrative, or making their voice come through clearly. Participants should be willing to write regularly, discuss sample essays, read work aloud, exchange respectful peer feedback, and revise more than once. Students who are ready to reflect honestly, experiment with different approaches, and strengthen both storytelling and mechanics will benefit most.

learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Select and develop an authentic personal story for a college application prompt • Organize a focused essay using narrative structure, voice, and meaningful reflection • Revise a draft for clarity, coherence, grammar, mechanics, and required limits Students leave with a revised college application essay draft, stronger writing and feedback skills, and clearer direction for future academic and application writing.

title: College Sports Marketing: Brands, Fans & NIL
raw_title: College Sports Marketing: Brands, Fans & NIL
subject: Business, Leadership & Entrepreneurship
price_note: The course detail page does not publish a course-specific tuition; campus-level range retained.
description_short: How does a college athlete become a credible brand? Students examine the business and media ecosystem of college sports, then study how name, image, and likeness has changed the relationship among athletes, schools, audiences, and commercial partners. Cases and discussion connect opportunity with legal and ethical responsibilities. The course moves from the
description_full: How does a college athlete become a credible brand? Students examine the business and media ecosystem of college sports, then study how name, image, and likeness has changed the relationship among athletes, schools, audiences, and commercial partners. Cases and discussion connect opportunity with legal and ethical responsibilities. The course moves from the landscape to personal brand architecture. Students define a story, values, audience, and point of difference, then plan content across social platforms. They analyze what brands look for in a partner, how sponsorship fit affects credibility, and why engagement strategy must serve more than follower growth. A Personal NIL Brand Pitch brings the work together. Each student develops a brand position, audience profile, content strategy, and potential partner fit, then presents the rationale with clarity and confidence. The project treats the athlete as both creator and decision-maker, emphasizing consistency, judgment, and responsible representation. Discussion, practice, and feedback help students check their reasoning and improve how they communicate the work. This two-week course takes place at Georgetown University. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by Georgetown University and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Map the business and media ecosystem of college sports • Explain how NIL changed athlete marketing opportunities • Define a personal brand story, values, audience, and difference • Build a cross-platform social content strategy • Evaluate potential partners for brand and audience fit • Create and deliver a Personal NIL Brand Pitch

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain the role of NIL within the college sports ecosystem • Develop a coherent athlete brand and content strategy • Evaluate partnership fit and present a responsible NIL pitch Students leave with a completed Personal NIL Brand Pitch and a stronger framework for athlete marketing, partnerships, and reputation.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and are interested in college sports, athlete branding, social media, marketing, content, business, or NIL. It fits athletes and non-athletes who want to understand how personal brands and partnerships are built. Participants should be ready to examine case studies, reflect on values and audience, create a content plan, and present an individual pitch. Students should be comfortable discussing both opportunity and responsibility in public-facing brand decisions.

learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain the role of NIL within the college sports ecosystem • Develop a coherent athlete brand and content strategy • Evaluate partnership fit and present a responsible NIL pitch Students leave with a completed Personal NIL Brand Pitch and a stronger framework for athlete marketing, partnerships, and reputation.

description_full: Why do prices rise, recessions spread, or markets react to unexpected news? Students use those questions to build an introduction to economic thinking and the U.S. economy. They examine supply and demand, inflation, market fluctuations, and the choices consumers and businesses make when resources and information are limited. The course connects microeconomics with larger institutions and policy. Students consider how stock markets, consumer behavior, and different economic systems affect growth and opportunity. They also study how government and central institutions respond to changing conditions, weighing the intended effects and possible tradeoffs of policy choices. Global interdependence adds another layer. Discussions and activities explore trade, international finance, jobs, resources, and the way external shocks can travel across borders. Students practice applying concepts to current and historical examples, explaining not only what changed but also which incentives, institutions, and relationships help account for the outcome. Discussion, practice, and feedback help students check their reasoning and improve how they communicate the work. This two-week course takes place at Georgetown University. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by Georgetown University and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Model how supply and demand affect prices and market behavior • Compare economic systems and the incentives they create • Examine inflation, recession, and consumer responses • Analyze government policy tools and their possible tradeoffs • Trace how trade and finance connect national economies • Apply economic concepts to an external shock or market change

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain core economic concepts using relevant real-world examples • Analyze how policy, institutions, and consumer behavior influence markets • Evaluate an economic development by identifying incentives, tradeoffs, and global connections Students leave with applied economic analyses and a clearer framework for interpreting markets, policy, and global change.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and are curious about prices, markets, government policy, business decisions, or global events. It fits interests in economics, finance, politics, international relations, data, or public policy. Participants should be ready to discuss competing explanations, work with basic economic relationships, and connect concepts to current and historical examples. Students who enjoy asking why outcomes change and considering tradeoffs will be well matched.

description_full: How do speakers turn an idea into a message people can follow? Students learn key concepts in public speaking and oratory communication while practicing speech making in a supportive setting. They examine topic selection, organization, speech writing, argument, and the relationship between a speaker and an audience. Guided practice helps students connect words with delivery. They work on verbal and nonverbal communication, prepare prompts, and consider how technology can support a presentation. Discussion and short exercises ask them to think before speaking, build knowledge about a topic, and choose an approach that fits the purpose. A persuasive speaking assignment brings the skills together. Students select an issue, organize a position, support it, and present to an audience. Feedback and reflection help them improve clarity and confidence while recognizing that effective speaking is interactive: good speakers also watch, listen, and adjust. This two-week course takes place at Georgetown University. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic exploration with campus life, growing confidence and independence, and clearer direction about interests students may want to explore next. The program is developed by Georgetown University and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Select a focused topic for a speech • Organize ideas into a clear beginning, middle, and conclusion • Develop reasons and support for a persuasive claim • Practice verbal and nonverbal delivery techniques • Use presentation technology to support a message • Deliver a persuasive speech and respond to feedback

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Organize and deliver a speech for a specific purpose and audience • Support a persuasive claim with clear reasons and relevant information • Use verbal, nonverbal, and presentation choices to improve delivery Students leave with a completed persuasive speech and greater confidence communicating ideas to an audience.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for middle school students who have completed 6th, 7th, or 8th grade and want to become more comfortable speaking in class, presenting ideas, or building persuasive arguments. It fits interests in debate, theater, leadership, writing, media, or civic discussion. Participants should be ready to choose topics, practice aloud, listen to classmates, and use feedback to revise. No previous public-speaking or debate experience is required. Students do not need to begin as confident speakers; a willingness to participate and improve is the most important fit.

learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Organize and deliver a speech for a specific purpose and audience • Support a persuasive claim with clear reasons and relevant information • Use verbal, nonverbal, and presentation choices to improve delivery Students leave with a completed persuasive speech and greater confidence communicating ideas to an audience.

title: Forensic Investigation: Crime Scenes & Case Strategy

subject: Law & Government
price_note: The course detail page does not publish a course-specific tuition; campus-level range retained.
description_short: A crime scene cannot speak for itself. Students learn how investigators document, collect, preserve, and interpret evidence so that later conclusions can be tested. description_full: A crime scene cannot speak for itself. Students learn how investigators document, collect, preserve, and interpret evidence so that later conclusions can be tested. The course begins with forensic history, Locard’s exchange principle, scene safety, and the responsibilities involved in protecting evidence integrity. Hands-on work introduces crime-scene sketching, photography, fingerprint analysis, ballistics, blood-spatter patterns, trace evidence, and impression evidence. Students also examine simulated blood typing, time-of-death estimation using cooling, chromatography, toxicology, and the investigative questions connected to arson and explosives. Each technique requires careful observation and accurate recording. Evidence only becomes useful when the process is defensible. Students practice chain-of-custody thinking, compare what different evidence types can and cannot show, and bring findings together into a case strategy. The emphasis is on scientific reasoning, documentation, and measured conclusions rather than dramatic certainty. Discussion, practice, and feedback help students check their reasoning and improve how they communicate the work. This two-week course takes place at Georgetown University. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by Georgetown University and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery. A supplemental course fee of $95 applies.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Document a scene through notes, diagrams, sketches, and photography • Collect and preserve evidence while maintaining chain of custody • Compare fingerprints, impressions, and trace evidence • Examine ballistics and blood-spatter pattern evidence • Use chromatography and simulated blood typing in analysis • Estimate time of death and integrate findings into a case strategy

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Document and preserve a simulated crime scene using forensic procedures • Analyze multiple evidence types and explain what each finding supports • Construct a case interpretation that distinguishes observations, inferences, and limitations Students leave with forensic documentation, laboratory analyses, and a stronger understanding of evidence integrity and case reconstruction.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and are interested in forensic science, criminal justice, biology, chemistry, investigation, or law. It suits students who enjoy careful observation and using several types of evidence to answer a larger question. Participants should be ready to follow safety procedures, record details precisely, work with classmates, and explain conclusions without overstating certainty. Patience, curiosity, and respect for evidence are especially important.

learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Document and preserve a simulated crime scene using forensic procedures • Analyze multiple evidence types and explain what each finding supports • Construct a case interpretation that distinguishes observations, inferences, and limitations Students leave with forensic documentation, laboratory analyses, and a stronger understanding of evidence integrity and case reconstruction.

title: Forensics 101: Solve Crimes with Evidence
subject: Law & Government
price_note: The course detail page does not publish a course-specific tuition; campus-level range retained.
description_short: How can a small clue change an investigation? Students explore how scientific methods help people examine a crime scene and test possible explanations. The course emphasizes observation, evidence collection, documentation, and the difference between what a clue shows and what an investigator thinks it might mean. Hands-on activities introduce trace evidence,
description_full: How can a small clue change an investigation? Students explore how scientific methods help people examine a crime scene and test possible explanations. The course emphasizes observation, evidence collection, documentation, and the difference between what a clue shows and what an investigator thinks it might mean. Hands-on activities introduce trace evidence, fingerprints, handwriting, and photographic evidence. Students compare samples, record patterns, and use real-world case studies to see how several pieces of information can support or challenge a theory. Laboratory-style work builds care, patience, and attention to procedure. As the course progresses, students combine findings to solve age-appropriate investigative problems. Discussion and reflection help them explain their reasoning, listen to alternative interpretations, and revise a conclusion when new evidence appears. The focus is not guessing the answer first. It is building a case that another person can follow. This two-week course takes place at Georgetown University. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic exploration with campus life, growing confidence and independence, and clearer direction about interests students may want to explore next. The program is developed by Georgetown University and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery. A supplemental course fee of $95 applies.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Observe and document details in a simulated crime scene • Collect trace evidence using careful procedures • Compare fingerprint patterns and record similarities • Examine handwriting samples for identifying features • Study photographs for relevant investigative details • Combine clues to explain and defend a case conclusion

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Record observations and collect evidence using an organized process • Compare forensic samples and identify relevant similarities and differences • Explain a case conclusion using multiple pieces of evidence Students leave with completed evidence analyses and greater confidence using scientific reasoning to solve unfamiliar problems.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for middle school students who have completed 6th, 7th, or 8th grade and are curious about mysteries, science, evidence, or how investigators solve cases. It fits students who enjoy noticing details, comparing patterns, and asking what information supports an explanation. Participants should be ready to work carefully, follow directions, collaborate, and discuss more than one possible interpretation. No previous forensic science experience is required. Students who enjoy hands-on investigation and explaining how they reached an answer will be a strong fit.

title: Global Business & Leadership
subject: Business, Leadership & Entrepreneurship
price_note: The course detail page does not publish a course-specific tuition; campus-level range retained.
description_short: How can organizations create value while responding to global challenges? Students use the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals as a framework for examining leadership, business, and social impact. Case studies, discussions, guest speakers, and hands-on exercises show how companies and nonprofits connect strategy with needs in communities around the
description_full: How can organizations create value while responding to global challenges? Students use the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals as a framework for examining leadership, business, and social impact. Case studies, discussions, guest speakers, and hands-on exercises show how companies and nonprofits connect strategy with needs in communities around the world. Students study the 17 goals, select issues that matter to them, and translate research into visual communication. An infographic exercise asks them to identify meaningful data and explain why a goal deserves attention. They then examine executive summaries, mission, market context, operations, funding, and the choices leaders make when resources and priorities compete. The course culminates in a sustainable business or nonprofit plan. Students define the problem, propose a solution, outline implementation, and build five-year financial projections showing revenue, expenses, cash flow, and potential investor returns. Presentations require them to connect impact goals with a practical plan and respond to questions about feasibility and leadership. This two-week course takes place at Georgetown University. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by Georgetown University and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Connect the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals to business challenges • Research one global goal and create a data-based infographic • Analyze how organizations address social and environmental needs • Draft an executive summary and operating approach • Build five-year revenue, expense, and cash-flow projections • Present a sustainable business or nonprofit plan

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain how selected Sustainable Development Goals relate to organizational strategy • Develop a practical venture plan with impact and financial considerations • Present and defend a sustainable business or nonprofit proposal Students leave with an infographic, a developed venture plan, and experience connecting global purpose with practical leadership decisions.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and are interested in leadership, global issues, entrepreneurship, sustainability, business, or nonprofit work. It fits students who want to turn concern about a problem into a researched and structured response. Participants should be ready to discuss complex issues, work with data, collaborate on planning, use basic presentation and spreadsheet tools, and explain financial assumptions. Curiosity about how institutions create change will help students thrive.

description_full: Who has the authority to act when Americans disagree about rights, policy, or public priorities? Students approach that question by examining the constitutional structure of the federal government and connecting it to current domestic and foreign issues. Discussion emphasizes critical understanding, respectful disagreement, and the relationship between public events and course concepts. The course moves through the legislative, executive, and judicial branches, including congressional lawmaking, presidential power, federal agencies, checks and balances, and the Supreme Court. Students analyze major cases and explore the Bill of Rights through an assigned-amendment presentation. They also consider barriers to civic participation and the responsibilities of active citizens in a democratic society. A civic-engagement presentation asks each student to identify something they would like to change or improve. Classmates then evaluate whether the legislative, executive, or judicial branch has the constitutional or practical authority to address it. Visits to the United States Capitol and a local courthouse let students question Senate staff and a judge, connecting classroom analysis to institutions in action. This two-week course takes place at Georgetown University. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by Georgetown University and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Examine the powers and limits of Congress, the presidency, and the federal courts • Analyze checks and balances and significant Supreme Court cases • Investigate freedoms protected by the Bill of Rights • Present the importance of an assigned constitutional amendment • Debate current issues through respectful, evidence-based civil discourse • Develop a civic-engagement presentation about a desired change • Visit the United States Capitol and a local courthouse

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain how constitutional powers and checks shape the three federal branches • Analyze civil liberties and current issues using course evidence • Present a realistic civic action and identify which institutions can address it Students leave with completed civic presentations, direct exposure to government institutions, stronger analysis and discussion skills, and greater clarity about continued study, a possible major, or a pathway in law, policy, government, or civic work.

curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and are interested in American government, constitutional law, current events, civil liberties, public policy, or civic participation. It suits students who want to understand how institutions work and how people can engage them. description_full: Why do states cooperate in some moments and compete in others? Students are introduced to nations as actors in an international system and to the forces shaping their choices. Core concepts include anarchy, power, authority, levels of analysis, balance of power, and the theories used to explain conflict and cooperation. Historical and current cases give the concepts weight. Students consider nuclear deterrence, the World Wars, the Cold War, the Russian invasion of Ukraine, conflict involving the United States, Israel, and Iran, international organizations, and global environmental issues. Readings and discussion ask them to compare explanations rather than treat one account as complete. A foreign-policy discussion assignment turns analysis into advocacy. Working in groups or individually, students represent a political actor, use data to construct a coherent position, and present that argument persuasively. Final assessment and reflection ask them to connect concepts, evidence, and communication while recognizing the interests and constraints different actors face. This two-week course takes place at Georgetown University. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by Georgetown University and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Apply levels of analysis to an international event • Compare theories of conflict, power, and cooperation • Examine balance of power and nuclear deterrence • Analyze the role of international organizations • Investigate a global environmental or security issue • Build and present a data-supported foreign-policy position

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Use international-relations concepts to explain state behavior • Compare competing interpretations of a global conflict or policy problem • Construct and defend a coherent foreign-policy argument using evidence Students leave with a completed policy discussion project and a stronger framework for interpreting global events and institutions.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and follow world events or are interested in politics, history, diplomacy, conflict, environmental issues, or international organizations. It suits students who want analytical tools for understanding why global actors make different choices. Participants should be ready to read, discuss contested events, work with classmates, use data, and represent a perspective they may not personally hold. Respectful debate and willingness to compare explanations are essential.

description_full: Who helps a patient recover, prevent illness, or understand a diagnosis? Students explore medicine through the many professionals who contribute to patient care and community health. Clinical medicine, emergency care, biomedical research, public health, genetics, healthcare administration, ethics, and career pathways provide a broad view of the field. Interactive activities make the healthcare system easier to see. In a healthcare team challenge, students receive patient scenarios such as a broken arm, asthma attack, or diabetes diagnosis, then identify the physicians, nurses, pharmacists, therapists, assistants, and other professionals involved. Case studies and discussions ask them to consider how teams share information and make patient-centered decisions. The course culminates in a Healthcare Career Project. Students investigate one profession, explain its role and training, and connect it to their interests and strengths. Simulations, guest speakers when available, and hands-on projects help students move from a general interest in medicine to specific questions they can continue exploring. This two-week course takes place at Georgetown University. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic exploration with campus life, growing confidence and independence, and clearer direction about interests students may want to explore next. The program is developed by Georgetown University and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Build a healthcare team map for a patient scenario • Compare clinical, research, public health, and administrative roles • Discuss emergency care, genetics, and medical ethics • Apply problem-solving to age-appropriate healthcare cases • Investigate the education and work of one healthcare profession • Create and present a Healthcare Career Project

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Describe how healthcare professionals collaborate in patient-centered care • Compare several clinical, research, and public health careers • Research and present the role and pathway of a selected profession Students leave with a completed career project and a clearer picture of how their interests might connect to healthcare.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for middle school students who have completed 6th, 7th, or 8th grade and are curious about medicine, biology, patient care, research, or the many people who work in healthcare. It fits students who want to explore broadly before deciding which questions or roles interest them most. Participants should be ready to discuss patient scenarios respectfully, collaborate on team challenges, research a profession, and present what they learn. Curiosity, empathy, and willingness to ask careful questions will help students contribute.

subject: Law & Government
price_note: The course detail page does not publish a course-specific tuition; campus-level range retained.
description_short: On Georgetown University’s campus in Washington, D.C., students explore courtroom strategy in a city closely associated with law, policy, and public institutions. A trial is a coordinated process in which every role sees the case differently. Students examine the responsibilities of attorneys, defendants, witnesses, judges, and jurors, then study how legal t
description_full: On Georgetown University’s campus in Washington, D.C., students explore courtroom strategy in a city closely associated with law, policy, and public institutions. A trial is a coordinated process in which every role sees the case differently. Students examine the responsibilities of attorneys, defendants, witnesses, judges, and jurors, then study how legal teams prepare a hypothetical case. Jury selection and voir dire introduce the questions advocates use to understand a potential jury. Working in teams from a mock-trial packet, students develop opening and closing statements, prepare direct and cross-examination questions, and learn when evidence may be introduced or challenged. Practice sessions require them to make objections, respond to an opponent, and revise strategy as the case takes shape. The culminating mock trial puts preparation into motion. Students present arguments, question witnesses, manage exhibits, and respond in real time while maintaining courtroom procedure. Reflection and feedback connect courtroom performance with the critical thinking, problem-solving, teamwork, and public speaking skills that effective advocacy requires. This two-week course takes place at Georgetown University. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by Georgetown University and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Analyze the roles of attorneys, witnesses, judges, and jurors • Practice jury selection and the voir dire process • Develop persuasive opening and closing statements • Write direct and cross-examination questions • Introduce evidence and make appropriate objections • Prepare and conduct a collaborative mock trial

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain the sequence, roles, and strategic choices within a trial • Construct examinations and arguments from a hypothetical case record • Present and adapt an evidence-based case during a mock trial Students leave with prepared courtroom materials, mock-trial experience, and greater confidence in structured legal advocacy.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and are interested in law, debate, justice, acting, public speaking, or strategic problem-solving. It fits students who want to understand both the preparation behind a case and the challenge of presenting it live. Participants should be ready to read a case packet, collaborate closely, take on an assigned role, question witnesses, and speak before classmates. Careful preparation and respectful competition are central to the course.

learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain the sequence, roles, and strategic choices within a trial • Construct examinations and arguments from a hypothetical case record • Present and adapt an evidence-based case during a mock trial Students leave with prepared courtroom materials, mock-trial experience, and greater confidence in structured legal advocacy.

They review a mock-trial packet and learn how jury selection, evidence, testimony, and argument fit together. Teams begin by writing opening and closing statements. They then prepare direct questions that help a witness tell a clear story and cross-examination questions that test another account. Short lessons and small-group practice introduce common objections and the steps for presenting evidence properly. The class brings those pieces together in an intensive, age-appropriate mock trial. Students take assigned roles, listen for what happens in the moment, and use prepared materials to respond. The experience develops speaking confidence, careful reading, teamwork, and a stronger understanding of how courtroom rules support a fair process. Discussion, practice, and feedback help students check their reasoning and improve how they communicate the work. This two-week course takes place at Georgetown University. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic exploration with campus life, growing confidence and independence, and clearer direction about interests students may want to explore next. The program is developed by Georgetown University and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

description_full: How can money today support a goal years from now? Students build an accessible introduction to finance, investment management, and capital markets. They examine saving, interest rates, and the power of compounding before comparing how stocks, bonds, funds, and cryptocurrency differ in risk, return, volatility, and liquidity. The course turns concepts into decisions. Students define financial goals and time horizons, explore personal risk tolerance, and study why diversification matters. Research and simulation activities ask them to interpret company or economic news, distinguish expectations from outcomes, and recognize common behavioral pitfalls such as acting from fear or excitement. By the end of the course, students design a personal investment portfolio. Their choices must fit a stated goal, time horizon, risk and reward tolerance, and diversification plan. The emphasis is on responsible decision-making, patience, and explaining a strategy, not on promising a particular return. This two-week course takes place at Georgetown University. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic exploration with campus life, growing confidence and independence, and clearer direction about interests students may want to explore next. The program is developed by Georgetown University and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain compounding, risk and return, volatility, liquidity, and diversification • Compare common investment types in relation to a financial goal • Construct a diversified portfolio aligned with time horizon and risk tolerance Students leave with a completed personal portfolio plan and a stronger foundation for responsible saving and investing decisions.

Participants should be ready to compare options, conduct basic research, join simulations, and explain their portfolio choices. No previous finance or economics experience is required. Patience, curiosity, and a willingness to think beyond short-term headlines will support success.

description_short: Why do people think, learn, feel, and behave as they do? They compare theoretical frameworks and learn how psychologists turn questions about behavior into research that can be observed, measured, and critiqued. The course examines
description_full: Why do people think, learn, feel, and behave as they do? Students survey major principles and perspectives in psychology, beginning with the field’s history and scientific foundations. They compare theoretical frameworks and learn how psychologists turn questions about behavior into research that can be observed, measured, and critiqued. The course examines biological bases of behavior from neural and chemical processes to the central and peripheral nervous systems. Students then connect biology with development, learning, motivation, emotion, memory, cognition, personality, and social interaction. Examples and activities ask them to distinguish a plausible explanation from a claim supported by research. Research methods provide a thread across the topics. Students compare observational, correlational, experimental, and quasi-experimental designs, considering the strengths and limitations of each. By analyzing studies and theories, they practice asking what the evidence supports, what remains uncertain, and how psychological knowledge can be applied responsibly. Discussion, practice, and feedback help students check their reasoning and improve how they communicate the work. This two-week course takes place at Georgetown University. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by Georgetown University and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Compare historical and current perspectives in psychology • Examine neural, physiological, and chemical bases of behavior • Analyze learning, motivation, emotion, memory, and cognition • Explore development, personality, and social interaction • Compare observational, correlational, experimental, and quasi-experimental methods • Critique psychological studies for strengths, limits, and conclusions

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Differentiate major psychological perspectives and fields of study • Compare research methods and evaluate the limits of a study • Explain behavior using biological, cognitive, developmental, and social evidence Students leave with research critiques and a stronger scientific framework for interpreting human behavior and mental processes.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and are interested in psychology, neuroscience, human development, behavior, mental health, or research. It suits students who want to understand both major topics and how psychologists build reliable knowledge. Participants should be ready to discuss studies, compare theories, analyze evidence, and question conclusions thoughtfully. Students who are curious about people and willing to test intuition against research will be a strong fit. Success depends on careful preparation, steady participation, and respect for classmates’ perspectives throughout the course.

learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Differentiate major psychological perspectives and fields of study • Compare research methods and evaluate the limits of a study • Explain behavior using biological, cognitive, developmental, and social evidence Students leave with research critiques and a stronger scientific framework for interpreting human behavior and mental processes.

title: Public Health: Protecting Communities & Preventing Disease
raw_title: Public Health: Protecting Communities & Preventing Disease
subject: Medicine & Health Sciences
price_note: The course detail page does not publish a course-specific tuition; campus-level range retained.
description_short: How can a community prevent illness before someone reaches a clinic? Students explore public health at the intersection of medicine, policy, behavior, and the conditions that shape population health. Historical and modern cases introduce the field’s purpose, major institutions, and the difference between treating an individual and improving outcomes across g
description_full: How can a community prevent illness before someone reaches a clinic? Students explore public health at the intersection of medicine, policy, behavior, and the conditions that shape population health. Historical and modern cases introduce the field’s purpose, major institutions, and the difference between treating an individual and improving outcomes across groups. The course examines pandemics and other public health challenges, including the Spanish flu, sickle cell anemia, and COVID-19. Students connect epidemiology, sanitation, vaccines, immunology, prevention, and intervention to the way health problems are measured and addressed. They also evaluate health messaging and marketing materials for audience, clarity, credibility, and likely effect. A final project asks students to apply a public health perspective to a real-world problem. They identify an affected population, analyze contributing factors, and propose strategies that may improve health. The project emphasizes evidence, feasible prevention or intervention, and communication that respects the people a solution is meant to serve. This two-week course takes place at Georgetown University. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by Georgetown University and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Define public health and distinguish population from individual care • Examine historical and modern health crises • Connect epidemiology, sanitation, vaccines, and immunology • Identify prevention and intervention strategies • Evaluate health messages for accuracy and audience fit • Design and present a population-focused public health response

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain how public health addresses health at the population level • Evaluate prevention strategies and health communication using evidence • Develop a feasible intervention proposal for a defined public health problem Students leave with a completed intervention proposal and a stronger framework for understanding health through medicine, policy, and society.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and are interested in health, medicine, biology, policy, equity, communication, or global issues. It fits students who want to understand why communities experience different health outcomes and how prevention can work at scale. Participants should be ready to discuss sensitive health topics respectfully, analyze cases and messages, work with classmates, and propose an evidence-informed solution. Curiosity about both science and social systems is a strong fit.

description_full: Why do people remember some things, follow a group, or react differently in the same situation? Students explore foundational psychology through questions about thought, behavior, and social influence. They learn how psychologists develop theories and use research methods to study experiences that may feel familiar but are not always simple to explain. The course moves through neuroscience, learning and motivation, memory and cognition, social psychology, and health and well-being. Discussions and activities help students compare how the brain, past experience, goals, identity, and the surrounding situation may influence what a person notices or does. Students practice reading psychological claims carefully and connecting them to evidence. Rather than diagnosing themselves or others, they focus on concepts, research findings, and respectful discussion. By the end, they have a broader vocabulary for asking good questions about the mind and recognizing how context can shape behavior. This two-week course takes place at Georgetown University. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic exploration with campus life, growing confidence and independence, and clearer direction about interests students may want to explore next. The program is developed by Georgetown University and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Explore how psychologists develop and test explanations • Examine basic links between the brain and behavior • Compare learning, motivation, memory, and cognition • Discuss how social situations and groups influence people • Connect psychological concepts to health and well-being • Evaluate an age-appropriate psychological claim using evidence

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Describe foundational psychological concepts related to mind and behavior • Explain how individual and social factors can influence an outcome • Evaluate a psychological claim by asking how it was studied Students leave with a stronger vocabulary for psychology and a more evidence-focused way to think about behavior and social influence.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for middle school students who have completed 6th, 7th, or 8th grade and are curious about the brain, learning, memory, motivation, identity, or why people behave differently in groups. It fits students who enjoy asking questions about everyday experiences. Participants should be ready to discuss examples respectfully, consider more than one explanation, and learn how research supports a claim. The course is educational rather than clinical, and students are not expected to share personal experiences.

description_full: How do culture, institutions, and relationships shape individual choices? Students use the sociological imagination to connect personal experiences with larger social patterns. Topics include culture, childhood development, family and social relationships, deviance, race relations, population, sexuality and gender, and large-scale social change. The course also introduces sociology as a research discipline. Students compare experiments, surveys, field research, content analysis, and other quantitative or qualitative approaches. They examine ethics, literature reviews, hypotheses, validity, and reliability, learning how the design of a study affects the conclusions it can support. Applied exercises move from critique to design. Students conduct a short content analysis and develop a simple field-research proposal or project. By connecting theory, method, and observation, they learn to ask sociological questions carefully and to examine social claims without reducing complex people or institutions to stereotypes. Discussion, practice, and feedback help students check their reasoning and improve how they communicate the work. This two-week course takes place at Georgetown University. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by Georgetown University and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

curriculum_sections.body: • Apply the sociological imagination to culture and institutions • Compare quantitative and qualitative research approaches • Identify ethical issues in social research • Formulate a testable hypothesis and select measures • Conduct a short content analysis • Design a simple field-research project

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain how social structures and culture shape behavior and outcomes • Compare research methods for a defined sociological question • Design an ethical study with a testable hypothesis and appropriate evidence Students leave with a content analysis, a research design, and a stronger method for examining claims about society.

Students begin by comparing amateur, professional, and international sports, then apply contract and tort law to sporting-event scenarios. NCAA eligibility, recruiting rules, and the transfer portal provide a second set of fact patterns where one decision can change what is permissible. The course then moves into NIL agreements, Title IX, collective bargaining, and alternative dispute resolution. Students evaluate pay-for-play and recruiting questions, examine what happens when labor negotiations stall, and practice negotiation, mediation, and arbitration through a sports-agent exercise. Antitrust law, the MLB exemption, representation and marketability, and conflicts of interest show how legal strategy shapes the business of sports. Students brief a case, compare endorsement, licensing, sponsorship, copyright, and trademark issues, and spot ethical questions involving gambling, doping, safety, and technology. The course culminates in a final exam. This two-week course takes place at Georgetown University. Students may request an official Georgetown University transcript. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by Georgetown University and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

description_full: What happens behind the scenes before a team takes the field? Students explore the business side of sports, including how teams are organized, how players are evaluated, how contracts work, and how games become global events and community platforms. They compare the responsibilities of owners, general managers, coaches, agents, and other front-office roles. Each class combines short lessons with interactive decisions. Students use data in player-evaluation challenges, practice mock drafts and negotiations, examine contracts and trademarks, and explore sponsorships and name, image, and likeness. Team projects also examine international growth, brand partnerships, and the social responsibilities of sports organizations. No playing experience or prior business coursework is required. Curiosity about how teams operate is the strongest prerequisite. Success depends on careful preparation, steady participation, and respect for classmates’ perspectives throughout the course.

subject: Law & Government
price_note: The course detail page does not publish a course-specific tuition; campus-level range retained.
description_short: What makes countries cooperate, and what pushes them into conflict? Students begin by examining nations as actors in an international system and learning how power, security, institutions, and identity can shape their choices. They compare major perspectives such as realism, liberalism, and constructivism, then use those ideas to make sense of alliances, nuc
description_full: What makes countries cooperate, and what pushes them into conflict? Students begin by examining nations as actors in an international system and learning how power, security, institutions, and identity can shape their choices. They compare major perspectives such as realism, liberalism, and constructivism, then use those ideas to make sense of alliances, nuclear deterrence, diplomacy, and international law. Historical and contemporary examples help students connect theory to events with global consequences. Through readings, case analysis, multimedia, and discussion, they consider the Cold War, international organizations, environmental challenges, and questions of race, gender, and legitimacy in world politics. The goal is not to memorize one explanation, but to see how different frameworks can lead to different conclusions. For the culminating foreign policy discussion, students represent a political actor, gather evidence, and work in teams to recommend a government response to an international problem. They organize their reasoning in a foreign policy brief and present a persuasive argument to the class. This two-week course takes place at Georgetown University. Beyond class, students connect active academic exploration with campus life, growing independence, new friendships, and a clearer sense of what students may want to explore next. The program is developed by Georgetown University and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Compare realism, liberalism, and constructivism as explanations of world events • Examine alliances, nuclear deterrence, diplomacy, and international organizations • Analyze historical and contemporary issues through readings, cases, and discussion • Represent a political actor in a team foreign policy discussion • Gather evidence and develop a response to an international problem • Present and defend a persuasive foreign policy brief

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Compare major international-relations theories and apply them to global events • Analyze how power, institutions, identity, and competing interests shape foreign policy • Develop and present an evidence-based response to an international problem Students will leave with a completed foreign policy brief, experience presenting a team argument, and a clearer sense of which global issues they may want to explore next.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for middle school students who have completed 6th, 7th, or 8th grade and are curious about world events, diplomacy, politics, conflict, or how countries work together. It is a strong fit for students who enjoy asking why governments make certain choices and considering how the same issue may look from several perspectives. Students should be ready to read, discuss ideas, work with a team, and support an argument with evidence. Curiosity and a willingness to listen, question assumptions, and revise an idea are more important than already having firm opinions about international affairs.

description_full: Good engineering research begins before anything is built. It starts with a question that is specific enough to investigate and important enough to pursue. Students learn how researchers move from a broad interest to a defensible question, a workable method, and a clear plan for gathering evidence. Through literature analysis, research-design exercises, case studies, and proposal workshops, students compare qualitative, quantitative, and mixed methods. They practice evaluating source quality, considering ethics, defining variables, and selecting methods that fit an engineering problem. Feedback from peers and the instructor helps students narrow the scope of their ideas and strengthen the logic behind each decision. This hybrid academy combines an on-campus experience with Polygence’s Core Research Program. During the campus program, each student develops an engineering research proposal, abstract, and professional scientific poster, then presents the work in a symposium-style setting. Afterward, students join a virtual cohort and are matched 1:1 with a Polygence research mentor in their field of interest. Across 10 virtual sessions, the mentor helps each student continue the project at an individual pace toward a research paper, symposium presentation, podcast, or another appropriate final format. This two-week full-day academy is part of Summer Discovery at UC Berkeley, held on the university’s campus. Students spend the full program focused on one intensive academy. The academy is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Narrow a broad engineering interest into a focused research question • Evaluate scientific literature and distinguish stronger from weaker sources • Compare quantitative, qualitative, and mixed research methods • Design a study with appropriate variables, evidence, and ethical safeguards • Draft and revise an abstract, research proposal, and scientific poster • Present the project in a symposium-style session with peer questions • Continue the project through Polygence’s Core Research Program and 10 one-to-one virtual mentor sessions

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Formulate a focused engineering research question grounded in existing evidence • Select and justify research methods appropriate to a proposed investigation • Communicate a research plan through an abstract, proposal, poster, and oral presentation Students will leave the campus program with an engineering research proposal and scientific poster, a plan for continuing the project through Polygence mentorship, stronger research and presentation skills, and clearer direction for further study.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This academy is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and are curious about how engineers investigate unanswered questions. It suits students considering engineering, applied science, technology, or design and those who want to test whether research is a good fit before committing to a longer project. No finished research idea is required at the start. Students should be willing to read technical material, refine a question, explain their reasoning, and revise work after feedback. The course is especially useful for students who enjoy asking why a system works, how it could be improved, and what evidence would be needed to support a solution. Students should also be ready to continue after the campus program through 10 one-to-one virtual sessions with a Polygence mentor matched to their field of interest.

description_short: How can a robot sense its environment and act on a real need? Students trace the history of robotics from early mechanisms to industrial systems, soft robotics, autonomous machines, and AI-driven automation. Examples from healthcare, manufacturing, architecture, space exploration, and disaster response show how design choices depend on the problem being solv
description_full: How can a robot sense its environment and act on a real need? Students trace the history of robotics from early mechanisms to industrial systems, soft robotics, autonomous machines, and AI-driven automation. Examples from healthcare, manufacturing, architecture, space exploration, and disaster response show how design choices depend on the problem being solved. Hands-on work introduces circuitry, sensors, mechanical design, building, and programming. Students assemble and code robotic systems, experiment with an XRP robot, and explore soft-robotics fabrication. Guided practice and testing help them see how hardware, software, and physical constraints interact when a system does not behave as planned. For the capstone, teams identify a real-world problem, research stakeholders, write a focused problem statement, and propose an innovative robotic solution. They develop the design, consider function and constraints, and present how the robot could address the need. Industry speakers and visits, when available, add context from the Bay Area robotics ecosystem. This two-week full-day academy is part of Summer Discovery at UC Berkeley, held on the university’s campus. Students spend the full program focused on one intensive academy. The academy is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. A supplemental course fee of $195 applies.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Trace major milestones and emerging trends in robotics • Build and program an XRP robotic system • Connect circuitry and sensors to physical behavior • Experiment with mechanical design and soft robotics • Research stakeholders and define a real-world problem • Design and present an innovative robotic solution

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain how mechanical, electronic, and computational elements form a robotic system • Build and program a robot to complete defined behaviors • Develop and defend a stakeholder-centered robotic solution Students leave with built robotic systems, code, and a capstone proposal connecting engineering choices to a real-world need.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This academy is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and are interested in robotics, engineering, coding, design, automation, or applied problem-solving. It fits students who want to understand both how robots work and why particular systems are built. Participants should be ready to build, program, troubleshoot, collaborate, and present a team solution. No prior robotics experience is required. Persistence is important because testing and revision are expected parts of engineering work. Success depends on careful preparation, steady participation, and respect for classmates’ perspectives throughout the course.

learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain how mechanical, electronic, and computational elements form a robotic system • Build and program a robot to complete defined behaviors • Develop and defend a stakeholder-centered robotic solution Students leave with built robotic systems, code, and a capstone proposal connecting engineering choices to a real-world need.

description_full: A strong business idea starts with a problem worth solving. Students begin by looking for unmet needs, testing whether an idea creates real value and narrowing their thinking to one original venture concept. Using the NFTE curriculum, they organize the idea with a Lean Business Model Canvas. Market research helps them define a target customer, estimate demand and understand buying patterns. Competitive analysis and a SWOT evaluation sharpen the value proposition, while branding and marketing workshops turn that strategy into a message customers can understand. Students then examine fixed and variable costs, pricing, revenue models and the point where a business can break even. They assemble their research and decisions into a professional pitch deck, practice answering questions and revise their work through peer and instructor feedback. The course culminates in a Fast Pitch Challenge evaluated with NFTE’s official rubric. Along the way, students consider how entrepreneurial choices affect customers and communities, adding responsibility and impact to the venture discussion. This two-week full-day academy is part of Summer Discovery at UC Berkeley, held on the university’s campus. Students spend the full program focused on one intensive academy. The academy is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next.

curriculum_sections.body: • Identify an unmet need and shape it into an original business concept • Organize the venture using a Lean Business Model Canvas • Conduct market research and define a target customer • Analyze competitors, complete a SWOT review and refine a value proposition • Calculate costs, pricing, revenue and a basic break-even point • Build a pitch deck and present the venture in a Fast Pitch Challenge

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Evaluate a real-world problem as a possible business opportunity • Apply market, competition and financial evidence to a Lean Business Model Canvas • Present and defend an original venture through a structured business pitch Students leave with a course completion certificate, market research, a completed Lean Canvas, a professional pitch deck, deeper venture-building skills, and greater clarity about continued study, a possible major, or an entrepreneurship pathway.

Startup teams compare traditional and social-enterprise models, study global venture cases, and develop a solution around the needs of a defined customer or stakeholder group. Their final proposal includes the issue, solution, business model, outreach and marketing plan, measures of impact, budget, and financing request. subject: Medicine & Health Sciences
