description_full: A healthcare breakthrough often begins with a carefully framed question. Students choose a topic in medicine or public health, examine what researchers already know, and learn how to turn an area of interest into a focused study that could produce useful evidence. The academy introduces literature review, research ethics, qualitative and quantitative methods, data collection, analysis, and community-engaged research. Students practice writing PICO questions, evaluate source quality through a literature scavenger hunt, work through a data challenge, and consider the budget and ethical choices behind clinical research. Abstract and visual-data workshops help them communicate the logic of a study clearly. This hybrid academy combines an on-campus experience with Polygence’s Core Research Program. During the campus program, each student develops a medical research proposal, abstract, and professional scientific poster, then presents the work in a symposium-style setting. Afterward, students join a virtual cohort and are matched 1:1 with a Polygence research mentor in their field of interest. Across 10 virtual sessions, the mentor helps each student continue the project at an individual pace toward a research paper, symposium presentation, podcast, or another appropriate final format. This two-week full-day academy is part of Summer Discovery at UC Berkeley, held on the university’s campus. Students spend the full program focused on one intensive academy. The academy is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Build a medical research timeline and investigate how evidence develops • Search and evaluate scientific literature for quality and relevance • Formulate a focused research question using the PICO framework • Design a study and address data, budget, and ethical considerations • Write an abstract and create visual material for a scientific poster • Present and defend a proposal in a mock research symposium • Continue the project through Polygence’s Core Research Program and 10 one-to-one virtual mentor sessions

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Formulate a researchable medicine or public-health question from scientific literature • Design and justify an ethical study using appropriate methods and data • Communicate a research proposal through an abstract, poster, and oral presentation Students will leave the campus program with a medical research proposal and scientific poster, a plan for continuing the project through Polygence mentorship, stronger evidence and communication skills, and clearer direction for further study.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This academy is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and want to investigate how medical and public-health knowledge is produced. It fits students interested in medicine, biology, epidemiology, health policy, data, or research and those who want to test an academic interest through a substantial independent proposal. Students do not need a completed research question before arriving. They should be ready to read scientific material, work steadily on one topic, revise after feedback, and discuss ethics with care. The course is a strong fit for students who enjoy asking what evidence supports a healthcare claim and how a better study could answer what remains uncertain. Students should also be ready to continue after the campus program through 10 one-to-one virtual sessions with a Polygence mentor matched to their field of interest.

learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Formulate a researchable medicine or public-health question from scientific literature • Design and justify an ethical study using appropriate methods and data • Communicate a research proposal through an abstract, poster, and oral presentation Students will leave the campus program with a medical research proposal and scientific poster, a plan for continuing the project through Polygence mentorship, stronger evidence and communication skills, and clearer direction for further study.

description_full: What technical skill, teamwork, and preparation does healthcare demand? Students explore the field through action-based simulations led by experts. Suturing, dissection, trauma response, clinical diagnostic simulations, case studies, and discussion introduce both the practical and interpersonal demands of health professions. Clinical scenarios require students to think across disciplines. They analyze information, propose responses, and consider how different professionals contribute to patient care. The course also compares pathways through undergraduate, graduate, and postgraduate study, helping students see how medicine, nursing, physician-assistant practice, research, and healthcare administration involve different preparation and responsibilities. For the capstone, students design a case-based presentation focused on a chosen health profession. Fictional cases trace people from diverse backgrounds through academic choices, extracurricular preparation, specialization, research, entrepreneurship, leadership, wellness, and public-health challenges. Each student develops and presents at least one case within a team format. Discussion, practice, and feedback help students check their reasoning and improve how they communicate the work. description_full: A patient’s symptoms may point in several directions. Students learn to ask what the brain, behavior, history, and environment reveal together before considering a diagnosis or treatment approach. That clinical lens connects neuroscience fundamentals with the realities of mental healthcare. Students map neurotransmitters and neural pathways, examine brain anatomy in a guided lab, and work through cases involving dementia, psychosis, mood disorders, trauma, eating disorders, and substance use. Role-play and simulations place them in the work of patient interviewing, mental status examination, ethics review, and multidisciplinary treatment planning. Discussions also challenge stigma and compare clinical evidence with simplified media portrayals. Across the academy, students reflect on the strengths, knowledge, and next steps involved in exploring a brain-science health career. Their capstone brings that reflection into a practical plan, which they develop with structured work time and present to classmates and instructors. Repeated case discussions help them connect scientific detail with careful, humane communication across different clinical perspectives. This two-week full-day academy is part of Summer Discovery at UC Berkeley, held on the university’s campus. Students spend the full program focused on one intensive academy. The academy is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next.

curriculum_sections.body: • Map neurotransmitters and connect neural pathways to clinical conditions • Examine brain anatomy through a guided laboratory activity • Conduct a patient interview and complete a mental status examination • Evaluate psychiatry cases in an ethics board simulation • Design multidisciplinary treatment plans for complex patient scenarios • Present a capstone plan for continued exploration of brain-science careers

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain how neural mechanisms and clinical evidence inform mental-health assessment • Apply ethical and multidisciplinary reasoning to patient cases and treatment plans • Conduct and communicate a structured analysis of a psychiatric scenario Students will leave with clinical case work and a personal exploration plan, deeper neuroscience and communication skills, and greater clarity about continued study or careers in brain science and healthcare.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This academy is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and are interested in the brain, mental health, medicine, or the decisions clinicians make when a case is complex. It can help students compare possible directions in psychiatry, neuroscience, psychology, public health, and related health fields. No clinical experience is expected. Students should be prepared to participate respectfully in role-play, case discussion, group planning, and presentations. The course addresses serious themes, including mental illness, trauma, eating disorders, and substance use. Students and families should consider the course’s mature subject matter when deciding whether the experience is a good fit.

learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain how neural mechanisms and clinical evidence inform mental-health assessment • Apply ethical and multidisciplinary reasoning to patient cases and treatment plans • Conduct and communicate a structured analysis of a psychiatric scenario Students will leave with clinical case work and a personal exploration plan, deeper neuroscience and communication skills, and greater clarity about continued study or careers in brain science and healthcare.

description_full: ACT/SAT Success Studio is a specialized test-prep course delivered by ESM Prep as part of the program held on UCLA’s campus. Before the program, students complete a questionnaire that helps ESM Prep create a personalized study plan around their goals, current strengths, and the areas that need the most attention. During dedicated two-hour sessions, students prepare for the ACT or SAT through a plan built for them rather than a one-size-fits-all class. An ESM Prep mentor is present at each session to provide one-on-one instruction, answer questions, and tailor support to each student. Students practice test-taking strategies, target important concepts in math and grammar, and develop a pacing plan for working through each exam. Individual feedback helps them identify which approaches are working and where more practice will make the greatest difference. The focused format allows students to make meaningful progress while participating in the broader program experience. At the end of the program, each student receives a recommended plan from ESM Prep for continuing their preparation at home. This three-week specialized test-prep course is delivered by ESM Prep on UCLA’s campus in Los Angeles, California. It is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by UCLA and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

Projects make the machine-learning pipeline concrete. Students customize a chatbot, analyze real-world data, and explore a decision-tree model that predicts heart-disease risk. Additional examples may include crop-yield prediction, movie recommendations, autonomous vehicles, social robots, or tools for disaster relief. Ethical discussions ask who benefits, who may be excluded, and what can go wrong when data or design assumptions are weak. For the collaborative capstone, teams select a meaningful problem and develop an AI application or prototype. They define the goal, prepare or interpret data, test a model, evaluate limitations, and present both the technical approach and the intended social impact. This three-week course is part of Summer Discovery’s Institute for the Gifted program on UCLA’s campus. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect active academic exploration with campus life, growing independence, new friendships, and a clearer sense of what students may want to explore next.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for middle school students who have completed 6th, 7th, or 8th grade and are curious about coding, artificial intelligence, data, or how technology can address real problems. Students should be ready to work through coding errors, collaborate on a project, discuss ethical questions, and explain what a model can and cannot do. A strong participant brings curiosity, patience, and a willingness to revise. The most important preparation is readiness to ask questions and take part.

description_full: Two patients may share a symptom and still require different diagnoses. Students learn to look past a single clue, compare the full pattern and ask what evidence separates one psychological disorder from another. The course examines mood, anxiety, personality, psychotic, trauma-related, eating and neurocognitive disorders. Case studies challenge students to apply DSM-5-TR criteria, while differential-diagnosis activities ask them to distinguish closely related conditions such as Bipolar I, Bipolar II and major depressive disorder. Students also compare psychodynamic, Adlerian, cognitive behavioral, narrative and Gestalt explanations of symptoms. A psychological-assessment role-play shows how clinicians gather and interpret information, including the limits and complexity of diagnosis. Students practice holding multiple hypotheses and revising a conclusion when new details change the case. That discipline matters throughout the capstone. For the capstone, each student selects a fictional or nonfictional character, studies the character’s history and symptoms, builds an evidence-supported diagnosis and presents the analysis in a paper or presentation. This three-week course takes place at UCLA. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by UCLA and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Compare major categories of psychological disorders using DSM-5-TR criteria • Analyze hypothetical clients through individual and group case studies • Practice differential diagnosis between disorders with overlapping symptoms • Compare psychodynamic, Adlerian, cognitive behavioral, narrative and Gestalt viewpoints • Explore psychological assessment through a case-based role-play and inventory • Diagnose a selected character and present an evidence-supported capstone analysis

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Differentiate major psychological disorders using symptoms, history and diagnostic criteria • Compare how several psychological orientations explain symptoms and treatment • Construct and defend a case-based diagnosis using relevant evidence Students will leave with a course completion certificate, a diagnostic case capstone and greater clarity about studying psychology, mental health or a related clinical field.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and are interested in psychology, mental health, human behavior or clinical decision-making. It is especially relevant for students who want to move beyond introductory psychology and examine how professionals assess complex cases. Students should be ready to discuss sensitive topics respectfully, compare multiple explanations, read diagnostic criteria and support their conclusions with evidence. The class does not train students to diagnose people in their own lives; its cases and role-plays are structured academic exercises.

learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Differentiate major psychological disorders using symptoms, history and diagnostic criteria • Compare how several psychological orientations explain symptoms and treatment • Construct and defend a case-based diagnosis using relevant evidence Students will leave with a course completion certificate, a diagnostic case capstone and greater clarity about studying psychology, mental health or a related clinical field.

description_full: A logo may attract attention, but a campaign works only when the brand, audience, message and media support the same idea. Students begin by examining the Four Ps of marketing and the reasons familiar brands are memorable. They then create a company, name its product and design an initial visual identity. Market research and audience decisions shape a marketing plan. Students develop messaging, slogans and jingles, choose media channels and build creative assets with tools such as Canva, PowerPoint or Google Slides. They study advertising techniques through real campaigns, then write and record a 30-second radio spot or storyboard a television commercial. Public relations adds another layer. Students write a press release or crisis communication and consider how a company should respond when its reputation is tested. After observing marketing and advertising elements around the UCLA campus, teams refine their work and present a complete product, advertising and PR campaign as one connected system. This three-week course takes place at UCLA. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by UCLA and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Apply the Four Ps of marketing to familiar brands and an original company • Name a product and create its logo, identity and core message • Develop a marketing plan based on audience research and campaign goals • Write slogans and jingles, then select appropriate media channels • Record a 30-second radio ad or storyboard a television commercial • Create PR or crisis materials and present an integrated final campaign

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain how audience, positioning, media and the Four Ps shape a campaign • Create connected brand, advertising and public-relations materials for an original company • Present and justify an integrated marketing communications plan Students will leave with a course completion certificate, a brand identity, marketing plan, creative assets and final campaign presentation, plus clearer insight into possible study and careers in strategic communications.

description_full: An AI system can produce an impressive result and still raise difficult questions. Who was represented in the data? What should a person verify? Which decisions require human oversight? Students use these questions to explore how artificial intelligence works and how responsible ideas are designed. Hands-on work covers machine learning, computer vision, generative AI, prompt design, and media verification. Students run a human-versus-machine pattern simulation, test a no-code image model with Teachable Machine, compare prompt strategies, and build a checklist for identifying AI-generated media. Case debates and a bias audit introduce fairness, privacy, transparency, accessibility, and possible misuse. Students then develop an original AI for Good concept around a real problem. They define intended users, explain the system at a high level, identify required data, and create a visual prototype or storyboard. An ethics red-team review helps them strengthen safeguards before they pitch the concept and its limitations to a nontechnical audience. They also reflect on what responsible innovation demands from a builder. This two-week full-day academy takes place at UCLA. Students spend the full program focused on one intensive academy. The academy is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by UCLA and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Map everyday encounters with AI and identify the system’s role • Run a human-versus-machine pattern-recognition simulation • Test a no-code computer vision model with Teachable Machine • Compare prompts and verify claims in generated output • Audit an AI case for bias, fairness, privacy, and transparency • Prototype and pitch an AI for Good concept with safeguards

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain core ideas behind machine learning, computer vision, and generative AI • Evaluate AI output and system design for evidence, bias, privacy, and human oversight • Design and present an AI concept with clear users, benefits, limits, and safeguards Students will leave with an AI for Good concept and presentation, stronger evaluation and design skills, and greater clarity about continued study or careers involving artificial intelligence.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and want to understand AI beyond headlines and automated answers. It fits students interested in technology, design, media, ethics, healthcare, education, business, policy, or another area where intelligent systems are changing decisions. Students should be ready to test tools, question results, discuss difficult tradeoffs, collaborate on critiques, and explain an idea to a nontechnical audience. The course will appeal to students who want to explore what AI can do while taking its limits, risks, and human consequences seriously.

description_full: How would you design a replacement body part that must fit, move and work with a real patient? Students begin by building a life-size anatomy model, then investigate how stem cells, medical devices and engineering can help repair or replace damaged tissues and organs. Design challenges make each body system concrete. Teams develop a prosthetic limb, map how 3D printing supports artificial organs and compare treatment options for kidney failure. They build and test an artificial heart valve, model lungs, investigate liver function and create an ear trumpet while considering hearing technology. Vision simulations and a cochlear-implant discussion add patient experience and ethics to the engineering work. Students document designs and reflections in a science journal while building a capstone proposal for a new application of regenerative medicine. The final project explains the medical need, proposed solution, possible benefits and drawbacks, and connections to areas such as cost, law, education or technology. Students choose a presentation format and share the finished proposal with the class. This three-week course is part of Summer Discovery’s Institute for the Gifted program on UCLA’s campus. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic exploration with campus life, growing confidence and independence, and clearer direction about interests students may want to explore next.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Build a life-size body model and connect organs to their functions • Design a prosthetic limb and evaluate its materials and constraints • Research 3D-printed organs and compare kidney-failure treatments • Construct and test an artificial heart valve and lung model • Explore vision, hearing and cochlear-implant questions through simulations and discussion • Propose and present a new regenerative-medicine application

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain how selected organs function and how a medical device may support them • Apply an engineering design process to build and evaluate biomedical prototypes • Present a regenerative-medicine proposal that considers benefits, limits and wider effects Students will leave with a course completion certificate, a science journal, several biomedical models and a capstone proposal, plus a clearer sense of what they may want to explore across medicine and engineering.

curriculum_sections.body: This course is for middle school students who have completed 6th, 7th, or 8th grade and are curious about the human body, medicine, engineering or how devices can solve health problems. It is a strong fit for students who enjoy building, researching, testing ideas and explaining how a design works. Students should be ready to collaborate on prototypes, record observations, discuss patient and ethical questions respectfully, and develop a project across several checkpoints. The experience can help students identify which medical or engineering questions they want to explore next.

learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain how selected organs function and how a medical device may support them • Apply an engineering design process to build and evaluate biomedical prototypes • Present a regenerative-medicine proposal that considers benefits, limits and wider effects Students will leave with a course completion certificate, a science journal, several biomedical models and a capstone proposal, plus a clearer sense of what they may want to explore across medicine and engineering.

description_full: Passion can start a movement, but lasting change requires a strategy. Students examine how nonprofits, philanthropy, government, businesses, and community organizations approach complex social challenges. Human-centered design, systems thinking, and theory of change provide practical frameworks for moving from a broad concern to an action that can be tested and improved. Case studies and collaborative design challenges ask students to identify stakeholders, examine power dynamics, listen to community perspectives, and define the problem before proposing a solution. They practice creative problem solving, purposeful leadership, impact measurement, and narrative change. Each activity emphasizes evidence and collaboration rather than assuming that one idea or organization can solve a system alone. The work builds toward a student-led community impact day. Teams develop the purpose, audience, partners, activities, responsibilities, and measures that will guide the project. Students also craft a personal leadership narrative that explains the values and experiences they want to bring to future community work. This three-week high school program takes place at UCLA in Los Angeles, California. The program is developed by UCLA and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery. It is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what they may want to study or pursue next.

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Analyze a social challenge across stakeholders, systems, and power relationships • Apply human-centered design and theory of change to an impact strategy • Plan and evaluate a collaborative community action project Students will leave with a community impact plan and personal leadership narrative, stronger tools for leading change, and greater clarity about further study or pathways in public service, social impact, or community leadership.

Students should be ready to examine complex issues without searching for a quick answer, listen to different stakeholder perspectives, collaborate on a public-facing project, and take responsibility for part of a community impact day. Previous leadership experience is not required. A completed program application is required.

Students learn how biology, evidence and clinical tools help medical professionals move from an unknown problem toward diagnosis and treatment. The course examines cancer, diabetes, hypertension, kidney disease, meningitis, genetics and causes of death. Alongside the clinical work, students compare the path to an MD with other careers in healthcare and research. For the capstone, each student investigates a disease’s symptoms, transmission, diagnosis, treatment and prevention, then presents the findings on a research poster. The finished work connects scientific research to clinical communication and career exploration. This three-week course takes place at UCLA. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by UCLA and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

The finished work connects scientific research to clinical communication and career exploration. This two-week course takes place at UCLA. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by UCLA and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

description_full: A small change in measurement, mixing or temperature can completely change a bake. Students learn that lesson through repeated practice, moving from familiar recipes into doughs, meringues, custards and pastry techniques. Each bake connects ingredient choices and technique to structure, flavor and presentation. Students compare results and decide what they would change next. The course begins with no-bake cheesecake, brownies, cookies, muffins and strawberry shortcake. Each recipe introduces a useful skill such as accurate measuring, portioning, whipping cream, decorating or modifying a formula. Students then work with yeast and overnight dough while preparing pita, focaccia and French bread, along with hummus, tomato jam, butter and fruit jams. Later projects add more technical components. Students bake cupcakes with cream-cheese frosting, make pavlovas with crème anglaise and whipped cream, and prepare éclairs and cream puffs with pâte à choux. The sequence gives them experience organizing a recipe, handling ingredients and combining several components into a finished presentation. This three-week course takes place at UCLA. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by UCLA and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Measure, mix and bake brownies, cookies, muffins and shortcakes • Whip cream, prepare frostings and decorate finished desserts • Knead and shape pita, focaccia and French bread dough • Make hummus, tomato jam, fruit jams and fresh butter • Prepare meringue, crème anglaise and composed pavlovas • Bake éclairs and cream puffs using pâte à choux

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Apply accurate measuring, mixing, kneading and baking techniques across several recipes • Compare how different ingredients and methods affect texture, structure and presentation • Organize multistep bakes that combine dough, filling, sauce or decoration Students will leave with a course completion certificate, practical experience across breads and pastries, and greater clarity about continued study in baking, culinary arts or food entrepreneurship.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and enjoy cooking, baking, working with their hands or understanding why recipes succeed. It is a strong fit for students who want repeated kitchen practice rather than a demonstration-only experience. Students should be ready to follow food-safety and classroom procedures, measure carefully, work through multistep recipes and help keep a shared workspace organized. The course begins with accessible recipes and progresses into breads, custards, meringues and pastry techniques.

subject: Economics and Finance
price_note: The course detail page does not publish a course-specific tuition; campus-level range retained.
description_short: A company may be growing and still face a poor financial decision. Students learn to look behind the headline by reading financial statements, comparing ratios, and asking how a choice affects cash, risk, and long-term value. The course introduces accounting fundamentals, budgeting, forecasting, time value of money, capital budgeting, capital structure, stoc
description_full: A company may be growing and still face a poor financial decision. Students learn to look behind the headline by reading financial statements, comparing ratios, and asking how a choice affects cash, risk, and long-term value. The course introduces accounting fundamentals, budgeting, forecasting, time value of money, capital budgeting, capital structure, stock markets, and risk and return. Applied problem sets and financial cases give students practice using concepts rather than memorizing terms. They analyze company performance, build models in spreadsheets, compare investment opportunities, and participate in stock-market simulations and group decision exercises. The capstone examines artificial intelligence in finance. Students research how AI is used in financial modeling, forecasting, investment analysis, or decision support, then evaluate a real application and present the benefits and limits clearly. The project connects established finance principles to the tools changing how analysts work. Peer questions require them to support claims with finance concepts and distinguish a useful tool from an unsupported promise. This two-week course takes place at UCLA. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by UCLA and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Read core financial statements and calculate performance ratios • Build budgets, forecasts, and time-value-of-money calculations • Evaluate capital investments and corporate financing choices • Use spreadsheets to create and test financial models • Participate in financial cases and stock-market simulations • Research and present a real application of AI in finance

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Analyze financial statements and ratios to evaluate company performance • Build budgets and models for investment and financing decisions • Explain and assess an AI application in financial analysis Students will leave with applied financial models and an AI-in-finance presentation, stronger quantitative business skills, and greater clarity about continued study or careers in finance, accounting, or analytics.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and want to understand how companies make financial decisions. It fits interests in business, accounting, investing, economics, data, technology, or entrepreneurship. Students should be comfortable working with arithmetic, percentages, formulas, and spreadsheets. Participants will need to complete applied problem sets, interpret company information, discuss case decisions, and present research. The course is a strong fit for students who enjoy using numbers to explain what is happening inside a business and want to compare several possible directions across finance and analytics.

subject: Computer Science & Technology
price_note: The course detail page does not publish a course-specific tuition; campus-level range retained.
description_short: A secret message is a mathematical puzzle with a purpose. Students trace cryptography from Caesar shifts and substitution systems to the Enigma machine and the public-key ideas that protect modern communication. Each new cipher reveals both an encoding strategy and a weakness a codebreaker can exploit. Hands-on challenges include building cipher wheels, encr
description_full: A secret message is a mathematical puzzle with a purpose. Students trace cryptography from Caesar shifts and substitution systems to the Enigma machine and the public-key ideas that protect modern communication. Each new cipher reveals both an encoding strategy and a weakness a codebreaker can exploit. Hands-on challenges include building cipher wheels, encrypting and decrypting partner messages, using frequency analysis, and testing Vigenère and Polybius-based systems. Students connect those activities to modular arithmetic, matrices, prime factorization, number theory, and the way computers represent information. Historical cases show how cryptanalysis influenced events and how security standards change when technology advances. For the capstone, students design and analyze an original cryptographic system or complete an in-depth cryptanalysis project. They document the key, method, mathematical reasoning, strengths, limitations, and evidence from testing, then present their findings to the class. This three-week course is part of Summer Discovery’s Institute for the Gifted program on UCLA’s campus. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic exploration with campus life, growing confidence and independence, and clearer direction about interests students may want to explore next.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Encrypt and decrypt messages with Caesar and substitution ciphers • Use frequency analysis to test and break simple systems • Explore Vigenère, Polybius, Enigma, and public-key ideas • Apply modular arithmetic, matrices, primes, and number theory • Compare cipher strengths, weaknesses, and historical consequences • Design or analyze a cryptographic system for a final presentation

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain how major classical and modern cryptographic ideas protect information • Apply mathematical patterns and frequency evidence to encrypt or break messages • Design, test, and present an original cipher or cryptanalysis project Students will leave with encrypted work, documented codebreaking strategies, and a capstone that demonstrates mathematical reasoning and security analysis.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for middle school students who have completed 6th, 7th, or 8th grade and enjoy puzzles, mathematics, history, computers, or secret messages. It is a strong fit for students who like looking for patterns and testing whether a rule works in every case. No prior coding or advanced mathematics experience is required, though comfort with basic algebra is helpful. Students should be ready to calculate carefully, collaborate on codebreaking challenges, explain their reasoning, and improve a design after classmates test it. A strong participant brings curiosity, patience, and a willingness to revise. The most important preparation is readiness to ask questions and take part.

learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain how major classical and modern cryptographic ideas protect information • Apply mathematical patterns and frequency evidence to encrypt or break messages • Design, test, and present an original cipher or cryptanalysis project Students will leave with encrypted work, documented codebreaking strategies, and a capstone that demonstrates mathematical reasoning and security analysis.

title: Creative Writing: The Art of Storytelling
raw_title: Creative Writing: The Art of Storytelling
subject: Creative Arts
price_note: The course detail page does not publish a course-specific tuition; campus-level range retained.
description_short: What makes a short story feel complete even when every word has to earn its place? Students read like writers, examining how character, plot, setting, dialogue, point of view, voice, conflict, and metaphor work together. Short fiction and podcast discussions give the class a practical way to notice techniques that can strengthen their own work. Students deve
description_full: What makes a short story feel complete even when every word has to earn its place? Students read like writers, examining how character, plot, setting, dialogue, point of view, voice, conflict, and metaphor work together. Short fiction and podcast discussions give the class a practical way to notice techniques that can strengthen their own work. Students develop an original flash-fiction story of about 1,000 words. They practice outlining without becoming trapped by a plan, writing more precise dialogue, using active verbs, and cutting words that slow a scene. A one-minute pitch helps each writer clarify the central idea, while humor, simile, and metaphor exercises expand the choices available during drafting. Revision is treated as part of the creative process. Students submit a first draft, receive individual notes, make focused editing passes, and prepare their story to be read and discussed with the class. They also learn about places writers can submit finished work. This three-week middle school program takes place at UCLA in Los Angeles, California. The program is developed by UCLA and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery. It is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect active academic exploration with campus life, growing independence, new friendships, and a clearer sense of what they may want to explore next.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Read short fiction closely to identify techniques writers use • Develop character, setting, conflict, point of view, and voice • Practice writing precise dialogue, imagery, humor, similes, and metaphors • Pitch a story idea clearly in about one minute • Draft and revise an original flash-fiction story of about 1,000 words • Share finished work and respond thoughtfully to class discussion

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Identify and apply core fiction techniques in an original story • Revise prose for stronger verbs, clearer dialogue, and more purposeful detail • Discuss how specific writing choices shape a reader’s experience Students will leave with a revised flash-fiction story, a practical editing process, and a clearer sense of which forms of creative writing they may want to explore next.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for middle school students who have completed 6th, 7th, or 8th grade and enjoy stories, characters, language, or inventing their own worlds. It is a good fit for experienced young writers as well as students who want a more structured way to begin. Students should be ready to read short pieces, write regularly, discuss craft, share work in a supportive setting, and revise a story after receiving feedback. Curiosity and willingness to experiment matter more than having a polished writing style. A completed program application is required.

learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Identify and apply core fiction techniques in an original story • Revise prose for stronger verbs, clearer dialogue, and more purposeful detail • Discuss how specific writing choices shape a reader’s experience Students will leave with a revised flash-fiction story, a practical editing process, and a clearer sense of which forms of creative writing they may want to explore next.

title: Criminal Psychology: The Roots of Criminal Behavior
raw_title: Criminal Psychology: The Roots of Criminal Behavior
subject: Law & Government
price_note: The course detail page does not publish a course-specific tuition; campus-level range retained.
description_short: How can criminal psychology help explain criminal behavior and support efforts to prevent it? Students examine psychodynamic, biological, genetic, social-learning, cognitive, developmental, sociological, and cultural theories. Case studies help them compare these perspectives while exploring violence, aggression, substance-related crime, and the psychologica
description_full: How can criminal psychology help explain criminal behavior and support efforts to prevent it? Students examine psychodynamic, biological, genetic, social-learning, cognitive, developmental, sociological, and cultural theories. Case studies help them compare these perspectives while exploring violence, aggression, substance-related crime, and the psychological and environmental factors that may shape decision-making. The course places students inside the investigative process through hands-on activities and simulations. They examine fictional crime scenes, interpret witness statements and behavioral evidence, analyze cognitive distortions, map community crime patterns, and compare modus operandi with signature behavior. Profiling challenges and a Behavioral Analysis Unit simulation ask students to connect theory with evidence without treating any one explanation as complete. For the capstone, students serve as criminal psychologists investigating a fictional case. They assemble a Criminal Psychology Case File that includes a case summary, at least three theoretical perspectives, psychological and environmental factors, an offender profile, and prevention or intervention recommendations. Students may develop the work as a report, presentation, or digital portfolio, then present their conclusions in a five-minute evidence-based presentation. This three-week course takes place at UCLA. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by UCLA and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Compare major psychological, biological, developmental, and social theories of criminal behavior • Investigate a fictional crime scene using witness statements and behavioral evidence • Analyze cognitive distortions, environmental risks, violence, and substance-related crime • Map crime patterns and distinguish modus operandi from signature behavior • Develop an offender profile with prevention or intervention recommendations • Create and present an evidence-based Criminal Psychology Case File

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Compare psychological, biological, social, and environmental explanations for criminal behavior • Interpret case evidence and behavioral patterns to develop a supported criminal profile • Create and present a case file with evidence-based prevention or intervention recommendations Students leave with a completed Criminal Psychology Case File, stronger investigative and presentation skills, and clearer direction toward further study in psychology, criminal justice, law, or behavioral science.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and want to examine criminal behavior through psychology, evidence, and hands-on investigation. It fits interests in psychology, criminal justice, law, behavioral science, forensic investigation, or public safety. Participants should be ready to discuss violence, aggression, substance-related crime, and other sensitive subjects in a mature academic setting. They will work with fictional evidence, compare competing theories, participate in simulations, collaborate on case analysis, and present supported conclusions. Students who enjoy solving complex problems and testing ideas against evidence will be especially well matched.

learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Compare psychological, biological, social, and environmental explanations for criminal behavior • Interpret case evidence and behavioral patterns to develop a supported criminal profile • Create and present a case file with evidence-based prevention or intervention recommendations Students leave with a completed Criminal Psychology Case File, stronger investigative and presentation skills, and clearer direction toward further study in psychology, criminal justice, law, or behavioral science.

description_full: How can a collection of numbers reveal a pattern, test an idea, or support a prediction? Students begin by asking where data science appears in everyday life, then set up Anaconda and Jupyter notebooks to explore Python syntax, variables, expressions, and data types. Hands-on investigations make statistical thinking concrete. Students review mean, median, mode, and outliers through card-based activities, then use Pandas DataFrames to import, clean, slice, and analyze datasets. They practice removing missing values, isolating columns, creating bar graphs, pie charts, and histograms, and choosing labels and formats that make a visualization clear. As their skills grow, students examine correlation versus causation, consider how interpretation changes a data story, and explore introductory linear regression. Capstone checkpoints guide each student from selecting a dataset and question to building a documented Jupyter notebook with analysis, visualizations, and conclusions. The course concludes with presentations that explain both the findings and the reasoning behind them. This three-week course for middle school students is part of Summer Discovery’s Institute for the Gifted program on UCLA’s campus in Los Angeles, California. It is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect active academic exploration with campus life, growing independence, new friendships, and a clearer sense of what they may want to explore next.

description_full: How can mathematics help divide something fairly, explain an election result, or find the best route through a network? Students investigate these questions through discrete mathematics, a field built around countable structures, logical relationships, and problems with clear constraints. The course moves through game theory, fair division, election theory, arithmetic and geometric sequences, and several branches of graph theory. Students draw trees, test planar graphs, color maps, trace Euler paths and circuits, and explore matching in bipartite graphs. Later work introduces generating functions and number theory. Exercises, group discussion, and short checks ask students to show how they reached an answer, not simply report one. A capstone gives the sequence a practical purpose. Students select a real-world scenario, model the problem, propose possible solutions, identify factors that could affect the result, and present how discrete mathematics might support future solutions. Three checkpoints support research, application, revision, and reflection. This three-week course is part of Summer Discovery’s Institute for the Gifted program on UCLA’s campus. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect active academic exploration with campus life, growing independence, new friendships, and a clearer sense of what students may want to explore next.

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Apply discrete-mathematics methods to constrained problems and real-world scenarios • Analyze graphs, sequences, voting methods, and strategic choices • Model a problem, compare possible solutions, and present a reasoned recommendation Students will leave with a completed capstone analysis, broader exposure to advanced mathematics, and a clearer sense of which mathematical questions they may want to explore next.

description_full: Start with an engineering problem worth investigating, then determine what evidence could move it toward a solution. Students explore the research cycle through questions connected to areas such as biomedical devices, smart cities, sustainable energy, computing, and aerospace. A paper-bridge design challenge makes the process tangible as teams test constraints, compare results, and revise their thinking. Students learn to find and evaluate scholarly sources, choose among experimental, computational, design-based, qualitative, quantitative, and mixed methods, and consider ethics in data collection. During the campus program, each student develops an engineering research proposal, abstract, and professional scientific poster, then presents the work in a symposium-style setting. Afterward, students join a virtual cohort and are matched 1:1 with a Polygence research mentor in their field of interest. Across 10 virtual sessions, the mentor helps each student continue the project at an individual pace toward a research paper, symposium presentation, podcast, or another appropriate final format. This 2-week full-day academy takes place at UCLA in Los Angeles, California. Students spend the full program focused on one intensive academy. The academy is available to residential and commuter students. description_full: What turns a fashion idea into a product people recognize, want, and buy? Students examine the business behind design, tracing how trends, materials, pricing, sourcing, consumer behavior, branding, and merchandising shape what reaches the market. Current industry examples and brand analysis make each decision more concrete. Students build a trend board, compare the life cycle of fashion movements, identify fabrics, and map a product’s path through a global supply chain. Costing exercises show how materials, labor, transportation, and retail markup affect pricing. A mock buying challenge asks teams to balance a target customer, trend forecast, budget, and product assortment, while a social media challenge explores how brands position and promote a collection. The capstone brings these pieces together in a fashion brand launch. Students define a concept or mini collection, identify a target market, create a brand identity, plan products and pricing, and develop a merchandising and marketing strategy before pitching the idea to the class. This three-week high school program takes place at UCLA in Los Angeles, California. The program is developed by UCLA and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery. It is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what they may want to study or pursue next.

curriculum_sections.body: • Analyze fashion trends, brands, target customers, and global fashion capitals • Build a trend board using color, fabric, silhouette, and consumer research • Compare materials and consider performance and sustainability • Calculate product costs, retail markups, and pricing decisions • Map a fashion supply chain and make mock retail buying choices • Develop and pitch a fashion brand launch with merchandising and marketing plans

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Analyze how trends, consumers, costs, and supply chains shape fashion products • Apply branding and merchandising principles to a defined target market • Present a fashion brand launch that connects product, pricing, and promotion decisions Students will leave with a trend board and fashion brand launch proposal, stronger commercial judgment, and greater clarity about further study or careers in fashion business.

Students should be ready to research, work with numbers, collaborate on business challenges, and present a developed brand concept. Artistic drawing or sewing experience is not required because the course focuses on the commercial side of fashion. A completed program application is required.

Students also reflect on which studio methods felt most natural and which skills they would need to practice next with greater intention. This three-week course takes place at UCLA. description_full: How does a designer move from inspiration to something another person can wear? Students begin by creating a mood board, learning the elements of design, and sketching outfits on croquis. The process helps them connect line, shape, color, texture, and space to a clear visual idea. The course then moves into construction. Students identify sewing-machine parts, practice straight stitches, backstitches, curves, and pivots, and learn safety procedures. Fabric investigations introduce natural and synthetic materials, grain, drape, texture, pinning, and cutting. Each technique is put to work in a finished project rather than practiced in isolation. Students first sew and decorate a custom bowtie. They then learn zipper types and use a zipper foot to build a personalized pouch. The final vest project introduces reading a pattern, cutting panels, assembling seams, fitting, hemming, and edge finishing. This three-week middle school program takes place at UCLA in Los Angeles, California. The program is developed by UCLA and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery. It is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect active academic exploration with campus life, growing independence, new friendships, and a clearer sense of what they may want to explore next.

curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Translate a visual concept into fashion sketches and material choices • Use sewing tools and a machine safely to complete basic construction tasks • Follow patterns and construction steps to create finished fabric pieces Students will leave with a mood board, sketches, a bowtie, a zipper pouch, and a vest, plus useful exposure to both fashion design and garment construction.

Students should be ready to follow safety directions, practice techniques before using them in projects, work carefully with tools and fabric, and revise a piece when construction does not go as planned. A completed program application is required.

description_full: A short film starts long before the camera rolls. Students begin with story, character, and a clear logline, then translate the idea into screenplay pages, storyboards, crew roles, and a filming plan that a team can actually follow. Workshops introduce scene study, audition self-tapes, visual storytelling, producing, directing, camera operation, lighting, sound, and production equipment. Students analyze short films and scripts, revise a screenplay, build a schedule, and rotate through responsibilities in front of and behind the camera. Reviewing dailies helps the group decide what is working and what needs another take. Production continues into editing. Students shape an assembly cut, identify reshoots or voice-over needs, and refine the work through rough-cut and fine-cut stages. Music, sound effects, graphics, and pacing become storytelling choices rather than decoration. The course culminates in an original short film written, performed, directed, produced, and edited by the student team. A final review lets students discuss how their choices changed the story. This three-week full-day academy takes place at UCLA. Students spend the full program focused on one intensive academy. The academy is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. description_full: How does an idea become a finished film that an audience can watch? Students follow the creative process through film history, screenwriting, storyboarding, acting, production, and editing. Along the way, they learn how directors, writers, performers, camera operators, and editors contribute to the same story. The class develops three short films based on student ideas. Students pitch scripts, shape scenes, plan shots, and rehearse performances before moving into production. Because filmmaking depends on a full crew, students rotate through different responsibilities and learn how preparation, communication, and respect affect what happens on set. Editing lessons then show how pacing and sequence can change the meaning of recorded material. By the end, students have contributed to films from initial concept through post-production and can better identify which parts of the process hold their attention. The experience balances individual creativity with the practical work of making decisions as a team. This three-week middle school program takes place at UCLA in Los Angeles, California. The program is developed by UCLA and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery. It is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect active academic exploration with campus life, growing independence, new friendships, and a clearer sense of what they may want to explore next.

curriculum_sections.body: • Explore film history and the roles that bring a production together • Pitch story ideas and develop scripts for collaborative short films • Build storyboards that translate written scenes into planned shots • Rehearse and perform scenes while learning on-camera acting basics • Rotate through production responsibilities during classroom film shoots • Edit recorded material into finished short films

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain how pre-production, production, and post-production connect • Apply screenwriting, storyboarding, acting, and editing techniques to a film project • Collaborate across creative and production roles to complete a short film Students will leave with experience contributing to three class short films, practical exposure to several filmmaking roles, and a clearer sense of which parts of cinema they want to explore next.

Students should be ready to pitch ideas, take on different production roles, respond respectfully to feedback, and help classmates complete shared projects. A completed program application is required.

Case analysis introduces homicide investigation, criminal and
description_full: Evidence has value only when investigators can show where it came from, how it was handled and what a scientifically accepted test can support. Students begin with that connection between science and law, then examine how a crime lab identifies physical evidence and works to determine its origin. Case analysis introduces homicide investigation, criminal and civil law, search and seizure, interviews and the role of the penal code. Students study DNA analysis and the Innocence Project to see both the power of forensic evidence and the consequences of poor laboratory practice. Repeated work with chain of custody emphasizes documentation, contamination prevention and accountability. The course also examines the Seven S’s of crime-scene investigation: secure, separate, scan, see, sketch, search and secure evidence. Students consider tools ranging from evidence markers and forceps to alternate light sources, sifting screens and digital-forensics software. Research, laboratory-style exercises and class presentations connect evidence recovery to reporting and courtroom use. This three-week course takes place at UCLA. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by UCLA and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery. A supplemental course fee of $95 applies.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Analyze homicide and criminal-investigation case studies • Examine how DNA testing can identify or exclude possible sources • Document evidence movement through a defensible chain of custody • Compare presumptive tests, confirmatory tests and laboratory reporting • Apply the Seven S’s of crime-scene investigation to evidence recovery • Evaluate how forensic evidence interacts with law, courts and wrongful convictions

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain how investigators locate, preserve, test and report physical evidence • Analyze the importance of DNA, scientific standards and chain of custody • Apply a structured crime-scene process to a case or evidence-recovery scenario Students will leave with a course completion certificate, case-analysis and documentation experience, and greater clarity about further study in forensic science, criminal justice or law.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and are interested in forensic science, criminal investigation, law or the way physical evidence shapes a case. It is a strong fit for students who enjoy close observation, case analysis and questions with no immediate answer. Students should be ready to discuss serious crimes in an academic setting, keep careful records, compare legal and scientific standards and explain their conclusions. Students should be comfortable engaging with mature case material.

description_full: A crime scene contains more than clues. It contains evidence that must be noticed, collected, preserved, tested, and explained. Students learn how chemistry, physics, biology, and the scientific method contribute to forensic investigation, then apply those ideas through experiments, role-play, and case analysis. The class studies fingerprints, DNA, blood types and spatter patterns, injury evidence, ballistics, drug residues, fibers, and trace evidence. Students practice bite-mark comparison, test fingerprint methods, analyze simulated blood patterns, and use a pickle-stabbing lab to examine how injury patterns can support an interpretation. Small crime scenes challenge teams to collect evidence carefully and critique one another’s process. A group project develops throughout the course. Teams research a case, form a hypothesis, consider due process, and create a crime scenario for classmates to solve. Legal role-play introduces the perspectives of the defense, plaintiff, detective, and forensic scientist before final case presentations and peer review. This three-week middle school program takes place at UCLA in Los Angeles, California. The program is developed by UCLA and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery. It is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect active academic exploration with campus life, growing independence, new friendships, and a clearer sense of what they may want to explore next. A supplemental course fee of $95 applies.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Observe surroundings and classify different types of forensic evidence • Apply the scientific method to bite-mark and fingerprint investigations • Analyze simulated blood types, spatter patterns, and injury evidence • Examine ballistics, trajectory, drug residues, fibers, and trace evidence • Collect evidence from staged crime scenes and evaluate another team’s process • Build and present a case project for classmates to investigate

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Collect and document simulated evidence using an organized process • Apply scientific observations to compare competing case explanations • Present a case hypothesis that connects evidence, reasoning, and legal context Students will leave with a completed group case project, practical exposure to several forensic methods, and a clearer sense of which parts of science or criminal investigation they may want to explore next.

curriculum_sections.body: This course is for middle school students who have completed 6th, 7th, or 8th grade and are curious about forensic science, crime-scene investigation, laboratory evidence, or how scientific findings are used in legal cases. It is a strong fit for students who enjoy experiments, puzzles, observation, and debating what evidence supports. Students should be ready to work carefully with simulated evidence, collaborate on a continuing case project, discuss fictional crime scenarios respectfully, and revise an interpretation when new information appears. No prior forensic or legal experience is required. A completed program application is required.

description_full: Why do people form habits, react differently to stress, or remember the same event in different ways? Students explore psychology through the brain, major theories, human development, behavior, emotion, and age-appropriate mental health topics. Activities turn abstract ideas into questions they can observe and discuss. Students build a brain model, separate popular psychology myths from facts, and try a simplified conditioning game inspired by Pavlov. A lifespan timeline introduces development, while emotion charades and nature-versus-nurture discussions show how biology, experience, and social context can interact. Stress-ball construction and calm-down tools connect psychological ideas to everyday choices without treating the class as therapy. Later work introduces common psychological disorders at an age-appropriate level and examines how psychology is used in schools, sports, counseling, and other settings. Mini case-study skits ask teams to apply concepts to realistic situations. For the final project, students choose a real-life question and explain it through art, a skit, video, or short presentation. This three-week middle school program takes place at UCLA in Los Angeles, California. The program is developed by UCLA and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery. It is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect active academic exploration with campus life, growing independence, new friendships, and a clearer sense of what they may want to explore next.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Build a brain model and compare psychology myths with evidence • Explore simplified ideas from major psychological theories • Test learning and conditioning concepts through an interactive game • Examine development, emotion, social behavior, and nature versus nurture • Discuss stress, mental health, and psychological disorders at an age-appropriate level • Present a real-life psychology question through art, video, skit, or slides

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain selected psychological concepts related to the brain, behavior, and development • Apply psychology ideas to age-appropriate real-life scenarios • Present a focused question using evidence and an accessible creative format Students will leave with a final psychology project, exposure to several parts of the field, and a clearer sense of which questions about people and behavior they may want to explore next.

curriculum_sections.body: This course is for middle school students who have completed 6th, 7th, or 8th grade and are curious about the brain, emotions, habits, development, mental health, or why people behave differently. It is a strong fit for students who enjoy discussion, creative projects, observation, and connecting ideas to everyday life. Students should be ready to consider different explanations, participate respectfully in age-appropriate conversations about mental health, work with classmates on activities, and develop a final project around a question they choose. No previous psychology coursework is required. A completed program application is required.

description_full: A startup idea becomes more useful when someone tests the problem behind it. Student teams begin by identifying a real need, writing a focused problem statement, and conducting customer discovery through interviews or surveys. The venture takes shape through market research, customer personas, competitor mapping, and a Lean Canvas. Teams choose acquisition channels, develop a simple marketing plan, and build a minimum viable product as a paper prototype, digital mock-up, or other workable concept. Unit economics, pricing, cost structure, break-even analysis, and a basic financial model force each group to connect ambition with practical choices. The final stage is communication. Students craft a value proposition, build an investor pitch deck, rehearse a concise story, and respond to feedback. A Shark Tank-style showcase gives each team a chance to present its prototype, business model, financial thinking, and customer evidence in a live question-and-answer format. A written reflection helps students identify what they learned while working together as founders. This two-week full-day academy takes place at UCLA. Students spend the full program focused on one intensive academy. The academy is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by UCLA and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Identify a real problem and write a focused startup problem statement • Interview or survey potential customers and build target personas • Map competitors and complete a Lean Canvas business model • Create a prototype or minimum viable product mock-up • Calculate pricing, costs, margins, and a basic break-even model • Build and deliver a Shark Tank-style investor pitch

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Validate a startup problem through customer and competitor research • Build a Lean Canvas, prototype, and basic financial model • Present and defend a concise investor pitch with evidence Students will leave with a venture portfolio containing customer findings, a prototype, business and financial models, and a pitch deck, plus greater clarity about entrepreneurial study or careers.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This academy is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and notice problems, imagine products or services, or want to understand what founders actually do after an idea appears. It fits interests in business, technology, design, marketing, finance, social impact, and innovation. Students should be ready to interview people, share unfinished ideas, work through numbers, divide responsibilities, and revise a concept after direct feedback. The course is especially useful for students who want to test several entrepreneurial roles and learn whether they prefer customer research, product development, strategy, finance, branding, or pitching.

learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Validate a startup problem through customer and competitor research • Build a Lean Canvas, prototype, and basic financial model • Present and defend a concise investor pitch with evidence Students will leave with a venture portfolio containing customer findings, a prototype, business and financial models, and a pitch deck, plus greater clarity about entrepreneurial study or careers.

description_full: A courtroom argument depends on more than confidence. Students need evidence, a clear theory of the case, carefully planned questions, and the ability to respond when testimony changes the direction of a trial. In Hit the Gavel, students explore how attorneys, witnesses, defendants, judges, and jurors contribute to the legal process. Students examine ethical questions in historical case studies, practice legal research, and build skills in opening statements, direct examination, cross-examination, objections, and closing arguments. They take on roles for both the prosecution and defense, learning how the same evidence can lead to competing interpretations. The course culminates in a mock trial based on the fictional events in Holes. Teams investigate whether Camp Green Lake violated child labor protections, prepare witnesses and arguments, and present both sides of the case. A judge and jury then weigh the evidence and reach a decision. This three-week course is part of Summer Discovery’s Institute for the Gifted program on UCLA’s campus. Beyond class, students connect active academic exploration with campus life, growing independence, new friendships, and a clearer sense of what students may want to explore next.

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: - Build a legal argument using facts, research, and clear reasoning - Question a witness and respond to competing interpretations of evidence - Speak persuasively while listening and adapting during a live trial - Collaborate in courtroom roles and evaluate a case from more than one perspective Students leave with experience preparing and presenting a full mock trial.

curriculum_sections.body: This course is for middle school students who have completed 6th, 7th, or 8th grade and enjoy debate, public speaking, research, courtroom stories, or questions about fairness and justice. It is a strong fit for students who want to practice thinking on their feet while contributing to a team. Students should be ready to read case materials, take on courtroom roles, question witnesses, listen respectfully, and revise an argument as new evidence appears. Students must bring a laptop or compatible tablet, a charger, and compatible headphones. Institute for the Gifted eligibility requirements apply, and families must submit a completed program application.
