title: Introduction to Real Estate
subject: Business, Leadership & Entrepreneurship
price_note: The course detail page does not publish a course-specific tuition; campus-level range retained.
description_short: What does it take to sell a home or manage a residential property? Students build a foundation in real estate while comparing the roles, responsibilities, and daily resources used across the profession. Career exploration introduces the skills behind sales, leasing, property management, contracts, and client communication. Workshops make the process practica
description_full: What does it take to sell a home or manage a residential property? Students build a foundation in real estate while comparing the roles, responsibilities, and daily resources used across the profession. Career exploration introduces the skills behind sales, leasing, property management, contracts, and client communication. Workshops make the process practical. Students practice completing real-estate contracts, distinguish features from benefits, develop a sales pitch, and role-play parts of selling a house. Possible academic field trips which may include a visit to the Weiser Center for Real Estate broaden their view of the industry and the pathways within it. For the capstone, students choose between acting as a real-estate agent selling a home or as a leasing manager running an apartment complex. Teams organize the steps, documents, decisions, and presentation required for their chosen scenario. The project connects professional responsibilities with communication, financial awareness, and the role real estate can play in building wealth. This two-week Summer Discovery course takes place on the University of Michigan campus in Ann Arbor, Michigan. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Explore careers and responsibilities across the real-estate industry • Practice completing introductory real-estate contracts • Distinguish property features from customer benefits • Develop and rehearse a real-estate sales pitch • Role-play steps involved in selling a home • Complete a home-sale or apartment-management capstone

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain major real-estate roles and professional responsibilities • Apply introductory contract and sales concepts to a property scenario • Develop and present a plan to sell a home or manage an apartment complex Students leave with a completed real-estate capstone and a clearer understanding of sales, leasing, property management, and industry careers.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and are interested in real estate, business, finance, sales, property management, or how housing can function as an asset. It fits students who want to explore the daily work behind transactions and operations. Participants should be ready to work with contracts, practice client-facing communication, collaborate on a scenario, and present a final project. Organization, curiosity, and willingness to role-play professional decisions will support success.

learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain major real-estate roles and professional responsibilities • Apply introductory contract and sales concepts to a property scenario • Develop and present a plan to sell a home or manage an apartment complex Students leave with a completed real-estate capstone and a clearer understanding of sales, leasing, property management, and industry careers.

title: Mechanical Engineering: Structural Analysis & Design
subject: Engineering
price_note: The course detail page does not publish a course-specific tuition; campus-level range retained.
description_short: How do engineers turn physics and material properties into a system that works? Students explore mechanical engineering through structural and materials analysis, design, manufacturing, electricity, thermodynamics, and heat transfer. Lectures connect scientific principles with machines, energy conversion, transportation, and production. Hands-on work moves f
description_full: How do engineers turn physics and material properties into a system that works? Students explore mechanical engineering through structural and materials analysis, design, manufacturing, electricity, thermodynamics, and heat transfer. Lectures connect scientific principles with machines, energy conversion, transportation, and production. Hands-on work moves from foundational experiments to design decisions. Students investigate levers and pulleys, compare materials, build circuits, and test heat transfer and insulation. Simulations and workshops help them connect mathematical or physical models with the behavior of a real system, while peer feedback supports revision. For the capstone, students design and build a functional miniature calorimeter. They move through design, prototype, testing, and improvement milestones while documenting challenges and choices. The final presentation explains the design rationale, integration of physics and thermodynamics, system performance, and changes made after testing. Discussion, practice, and feedback help students test their reasoning and improve how they communicate the work. This two-week Summer Discovery course takes place on the University of Michigan campus in Ann Arbor, Michigan. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. A supplemental course fee of $95 applies.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Test foundational physics principles through levers and pulleys • Compare materials for structural and design decisions • Build circuits for an introductory mechanical system • Experiment with heat transfer and insulation • Design, prototype, and test a miniature calorimeter • Present system performance and explain design revisions

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Apply physics, materials, electricity, and thermodynamics to engineering problems • Build and test a functional device against defined performance criteria • Explain an iterative design process using evidence from prototype testing Students leave with a functional calorimeter prototype, design documentation, and experience connecting engineering theory with testing and improvement.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and are interested in mechanical engineering, physics, structures, materials, energy, manufacturing, or design. It fits students who want to build and test a working system. Participants should be ready for quantitative reasoning, hands-on experiments, circuit building, prototype development, troubleshooting, and presentation. Persistence and willingness to learn from failed tests will be valuable. Success depends on careful preparation, steady participation, and respect for classmates’ perspectives throughout the course.

learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Apply physics, materials, electricity, and thermodynamics to engineering problems • Build and test a functional device against defined performance criteria • Explain an iterative design process using evidence from prototype testing Students leave with a functional calorimeter prototype, design documentation, and experience connecting engineering theory with testing and improvement.

description_full: A healthcare breakthrough often begins with a carefully framed question. Students choose a topic in medicine or public health, examine what researchers already know, and learn how to turn an area of interest into a focused study that could produce useful evidence. The academy introduces literature review, research ethics, qualitative and quantitative methods, data collection, analysis, and community-engaged research. Students practice writing PICO questions, evaluate source quality through a literature scavenger hunt, work through a data challenge, and consider the budget and ethical choices behind clinical research. Abstract and visual-data workshops help them communicate the logic of a study clearly. This hybrid academy combines an on-campus experience with Polygence’s Core Research Program. During the campus program, each student develops a medical research proposal, abstract, and professional scientific poster, then presents the work in a symposium-style setting. Afterward, students join a virtual cohort and are matched 1:1 with a Polygence research mentor in their field of interest. Across 10 virtual sessions, the mentor helps each student continue the project at an individual pace toward a research paper, symposium presentation, podcast, or another appropriate final format. This two-week Summer Discovery full-day academy takes place on the University of Michigan campus in Ann Arbor, Michigan. Students spend the full program focused on one intensive academy. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Build a medical research timeline and investigate how evidence develops • Search and evaluate scientific literature for quality and relevance • Formulate a focused research question using the PICO framework • Design a study and address data, budget, and ethical considerations • Write an abstract and create visual material for a scientific poster • Present and defend a proposal in a mock research symposium • Continue the project through Polygence’s Core Research Program and 10 one-to-one virtual mentor sessions

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Formulate a researchable medicine or public-health question from scientific literature • Design and justify an ethical study using appropriate methods and data • Communicate and continue a research project through an abstract, poster, oral presentation, and individual mentorship Students will leave the campus program with a medical research proposal and scientific poster, a plan for continuing the project through Polygence mentorship, stronger evidence and communication skills, and clearer direction for further study.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This academy is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and want to investigate how medical and public-health knowledge is produced. It fits students interested in medicine, biology, epidemiology, health policy, data, or research and those who want to test an academic interest through a substantial independent proposal. Students do not need a completed research question before arriving. They should be ready to read scientific material, work steadily on one topic, revise after feedback, and discuss ethics with care. The course is a strong fit for students who enjoy asking what evidence supports a healthcare claim and how a better study could answer what remains uncertain. Students should also be ready to continue after the campus program through 10 one-to-one virtual sessions with a Polygence mentor matched to their field of interest.

subject: Law & Government
price_note: The course detail page does not publish a course-specific tuition; campus-level range retained.
description_short: On the University of Michigan campus in Ann Arbor, students explore courtroom strategy in a lively college-town setting. A trial is a coordinated process in which every role sees the case differently. Students examine the responsibilities of attorneys, defendants, witnesses, judges, and jurors, then study how legal teams prepare a hypothetical case. Jury sel
description_full: On the University of Michigan campus in Ann Arbor, students explore courtroom strategy in a lively college-town setting. A trial is a coordinated process in which every role sees the case differently. Students examine the responsibilities of attorneys, defendants, witnesses, judges, and jurors, then study how legal teams prepare a hypothetical case. Jury selection and voir dire introduce the questions advocates use to understand a potential jury. Working in teams from a mock-trial packet, students develop opening and closing statements, prepare direct and cross-examination questions, and learn when evidence may be introduced or challenged. Practice sessions require them to make objections, respond to an opponent, and revise strategy as the case takes shape. The culminating mock trial puts preparation into motion. Students present arguments, question witnesses, manage exhibits, and respond in real time while maintaining courtroom procedure. Reflection and feedback connect courtroom performance with the critical thinking, problem-solving, teamwork, and public speaking skills that effective advocacy requires. This two-week Summer Discovery course takes place on the University of Michigan campus in Ann Arbor, Michigan. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Analyze the roles of attorneys, witnesses, judges, and jurors • Practice jury selection and the voir dire process • Develop persuasive opening and closing statements • Write direct and cross-examination questions • Introduce evidence and make appropriate objections • Prepare and conduct a collaborative mock trial

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain the sequence, roles, and strategic choices within a trial • Construct examinations and arguments from a hypothetical case record • Present and adapt an evidence-based case during a mock trial Students leave with prepared courtroom materials, mock-trial experience, and greater confidence in structured legal advocacy.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and are interested in law, debate, justice, acting, public speaking, or strategic problem-solving. It fits students who want to understand both the preparation behind a case and the challenge of presenting it live. Participants should be ready to read a case packet, collaborate closely, take on an assigned role, question witnesses, and speak before classmates. Careful preparation and respectful competition are central to the course.

learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain the sequence, roles, and strategic choices within a trial • Construct examinations and arguments from a hypothetical case record • Present and adapt an evidence-based case during a mock trial Students leave with prepared courtroom materials, mock-trial experience, and greater confidence in structured legal advocacy.

title: Personal Finance & Investment Strategy
subject: Economics and Finance
price_note: The course detail page does not publish a course-specific tuition; campus-level range retained.
description_short: How can today’s financial decisions create more options in the future? Students build an introduction to budgeting, saving, credit, debt, investing, and entrepreneurship. They examine compounding, interest rates, stocks, bonds, commodities, and the differences between major exchanges while connecting financial choices to goals, income, time horizon, and pers
description_full: How can today’s financial decisions create more options in the future? Students build an introduction to budgeting, saving, credit, debt, investing, and entrepreneurship. They examine compounding, interest rates, stocks, bonds, commodities, and the differences between major exchanges while connecting financial choices to goals, income, time horizon, and personal values. Applied exercises move from concepts to decisions. Students compare the long-term effect of starting to invest at different ages, use simulated money to examine investment preferences, and consider how corporations manage capital. They also study responsible credit, financial integrity, transparency, and the tradeoffs involved in personal or business choices. For the capstone, students develop a personal financial plan individually or with a group. They research a career and realistic salary, set short- and long-term goals, create a monthly budget, plan savings and an emergency fund, explain credit and debt management, and outline an investing strategy. Housing, transportation, and a side-business idea complete the future scenario. This two-week Summer Discovery course takes place on the University of Michigan campus in Ann Arbor, Michigan. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Model how compound interest changes long-term outcomes • Compare stocks, bonds, commodities, and major exchanges • Develop a monthly budget from a researched career salary • Plan savings, an emergency fund, credit, and debt management • Test investment choices using simulated money • Create and present a comprehensive personal financial plan

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain how budgeting, credit, debt, saving, and investing connect • Evaluate financial choices using goals, time horizon, and relevant tradeoffs • Develop a realistic long-term personal financial plan Students leave with a completed financial plan and stronger tools for making informed decisions about income, spending, credit, saving, investing, and entrepreneurship.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and want to understand personal finance, investing, credit, budgeting, or entrepreneurship. It fits students who want practical tools they can connect to future goals. Participants should be ready to work with realistic income and expense assumptions, compare choices, use basic calculations, and explain a long-term plan. Careful thinking and willingness to revise assumptions will be valuable. Success depends on careful preparation, steady participation, and respect for classmates’ perspectives throughout the course.

learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain how budgeting, credit, debt, saving, and investing connect • Evaluate financial choices using goals, time horizon, and relevant tradeoffs • Develop a realistic long-term personal financial plan Students leave with a completed financial plan and stronger tools for making informed decisions about income, spending, credit, saving, investing, and entrepreneurship.

subject: Law & Government
price_note: The course detail page does not publish a course-specific tuition; campus-level range retained.
description_short: Why do people follow a crowd, obey authority, respond to persuasion, or act differently across social settings? Students examine the forces shaping behavior in groups, relationships, institutions, and daily life. Concepts include conformity, obedience, attribution, social norms, identity, stereotypes, prejudice, gender expectations, and social influence. Cla
description_full: Why do people follow a crowd, obey authority, respond to persuasion, or act differently across social settings? Students examine the forces shaping behavior in groups, relationships, institutions, and daily life. Concepts include conformity, obedience, attribution, social norms, identity, stereotypes, prejudice, gender expectations, and social influence. Classic studies, film and television clips, advertisements, social media, and public moments become material for analysis. Students identify invisible rules, break down the emotional promise behind persuasive messages, and compare research questions, methods, findings, implications, and ethical concerns in studies such as the Bystander Effect and Robbers Cave. For the capstone, students create a podcast examining a trend, public moment, advertisement, scene, social-media behavior, or everyday situation through at least two concepts. They pose a central question, use a vivid example, and explain both what the example shows and what it cannot prove. Discussion, practice, and feedback help students test their reasoning and improve how they communicate the work. This two-week Summer Discovery course takes place on the University of Michigan campus in Ann Arbor, Michigan. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Identify unwritten social norms across everyday settings • Analyze conformity, obedience, attribution, and group identity • Break down persuasive messages and emotional promises • Evaluate classic studies for methods, findings, and ethics • Apply social psychology concepts to media and public behavior • Produce a podcast using two concepts and one central question

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain how social context and group processes can shape behavior • Evaluate psychological research and media examples without overstating conclusions • Create a responsible podcast applying multiple social psychology concepts Students leave with a completed podcast and a stronger evidence-based framework for understanding persuasion, conformity, identity, and group behavior.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and are interested in psychology, persuasion, group behavior, identity, media, marketing, or social research. It fits students who enjoy examining familiar behavior from a new perspective. Participants should be ready to discuss sensitive social topics respectfully, analyze studies and media, compare concepts, and develop an audio project. Curiosity about both people and evidence will support success. Success depends on careful preparation, steady participation, and respect for classmates’ perspectives throughout the course.

learning_outcomes: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain how social context and group processes can shape behavior • Evaluate psychological research and media examples without overstating conclusions • Create a responsible podcast applying multiple social psychology concepts Students leave with a completed podcast and a stronger evidence-based framework for understanding persuasion, conformity, identity, and group behavior.

Students examine the forces shaping behavior in groups, relationships, institutions, and daily life. Concepts include conformity, obedience, attribution, social norms, identity, stereotypes, prejudice, gender expectations, and social influence. Classic studies, film and television clips, advertisements, social media, and public moments become material for analysis. Students identify invisible rules, break down the emotional promise behind persuasive messages, and compare research questions, methods, findings, implications, and ethical concerns in studies such as the Bystander Effect and Robbers Cave. For the capstone, students create a podcast examining a trend, public moment, advertisement, scene, social-media behavior, or everyday situation through at least two concepts. They pose a central question, use a vivid example, and explain both what the example shows and what it cannot prove. Discussion, practice, and feedback help students test their reasoning and improve how they communicate the work. This two-week Summer Discovery course takes place on the University of Michigan campus in Ann Arbor, Michigan. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next.

curriculum_sections.body: • Identify unwritten social norms across everyday settings • Analyze conformity, obedience, attribution, and group identity • Break down persuasive messages and emotional promises • Evaluate classic studies for methods, findings, and ethics • Apply social psychology concepts to media and public behavior • Produce a podcast using two concepts and one central question

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain how social context and group processes can shape behavior • Evaluate psychological research and media examples without overstating conclusions • Create a responsible podcast applying multiple social psychology concepts Students leave with a completed podcast and a stronger evidence-based framework for understanding persuasion, conformity, identity, and group behavior.

description_full: Why is sport both a major business and an important part of American culture? Students survey management issues and strategies shaping the industry, connecting fan participation and consumer behavior with the billions of dollars generated across teams, schools, media, sponsors, and events. Lectures, discussion, readings, video, and small-group case studies examine sports marketing and revenue alongside broader institutional questions. Students consider the financial implications of Title IX, the relationship between sport and race, strategies for reaching Generation Z, and the uniquely American business structure of intercollegiate athletics. Case analysis asks students to connect a management choice with its financial, social, and organizational consequences. The course culminates in a comprehensive assessment of the concepts and readings, requiring students to synthesize how leaders generate revenue while responding to the cultural and institutional responsibilities surrounding sport. Discussion, practice, and feedback help students test their reasoning and improve how they communicate the work. This two-week Summer Discovery course takes place on the University of Michigan campus in Ann Arbor, Michigan. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next.

curriculum_sections.body: • Examine why sport carries economic and cultural importance • Analyze marketing strategies and influences on consumer behavior • Evaluate revenue and management decisions through case studies • Study the financial implications of Title IX • Discuss the relationship between sport, race, and institutions • Assess the business structure of intercollegiate athletics

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Explain how marketing, consumer behavior, and revenue interact in sports business • Analyze institutional issues such as Title IX, race, and college athletics • Evaluate a sports-management decision using financial and social evidence Students leave with completed case analyses and a stronger framework for understanding the business, cultural, and institutional forces shaping American sports.

description_full: How does the structure of a joint shape movement, and how do the body’s systems work together to keep a person functioning? Students investigate human anatomy through state-of-the-art 3D models, moving from the nervous, cardiovascular, and lymphatic systems to the respiratory, digestive, urinary, and reproductive systems. The second part of the course brings anatomy into specific regions and professional settings. Students examine the head, neck, trunk, shoulder complex, arms, pelvis, hips, knees, ankles, and feet. Guest lectures from doctors and researchers add specialist perspectives, while a prosthetics demonstration shows how anatomical knowledge informs the design and use of assistive devices. Visits to the Stark Center, Dell Med, the Texas Science and Natural History Museum, and an imaging center help students connect models and classroom concepts with real facilities and technologies. Assignments, review activities, and a final exam reinforce the material. Students also prepare and deliver a PowerPoint presentation that asks them to organize anatomical information and communicate it clearly. This two-week full-day academy takes place at UT Austin. Students spend the full program focused on one intensive academy. The academy is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by the University of Texas at Austin and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery. A supplemental course fee of $95 applies.

curriculum_sections.body: • Explore the body’s major systems using state-of-the-art 3D anatomical models • Examine the head, trunk, limbs, and major joints by region • Hear guest specialists explain anatomy in medicine and research • Visit medical, imaging, science, and physical-culture facilities • Observe a prosthetics demonstration connecting anatomy with assistive-device design • Prepare and deliver a PowerPoint presentation on an anatomical topic

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Identify major structures across the body’s principal organ systems and regions • Explain relationships between anatomical structure, system function, and human movement • Organize and present anatomical information using models, evidence, and accurate terminology Students will leave with a completed presentation, stronger anatomical and scientific-communication skills, and clearer direction for further study or careers in health, research, or biomedical engineering. Students receive a University of Texas branded certificate of completion at the end of the program.

It is especially relevant for students curious about how anatomical knowledge supports clinical care, medical imaging, rehabilitation, prosthetics, or biomedical engineering. Participants should be ready to study detailed body systems, work with 3D models, learn from guest specialists, take part in facility visits, complete assignments and an exam, and present their work to the class. Applicants must also complete the program application.

description_full: How can engineering tools help researchers understand the body or improve healthcare? Students begin with the engineering design process and the major disciplines that contribute to biomedical engineering. Biology and cell and tissue engineering establish a foundation for examining how living systems interact with materials, forces, devices, and data. Each course topic opens a different window into the field. Students investigate biomaterials and biomechanics, then move into computational biomedical engineering, medical devices and instrumentation, organ-on-chip systems, and biomedical imaging. Laboratory tours connect these concepts with current research settings and the equipment biomedical engineers use. Quizzes and short reflection papers ask students to interpret lectures, laboratory activities, tours, and guest presentations. In teams, students prepare two presentations on engineering concepts or research topics. The sequence helps them compare biomedical specialties, communicate technical ideas, and consider the kinds of problems they may want to investigate further. This two-week full-day academy takes place at UT Austin. Students spend the full program focused on one intensive academy. The academy is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by the University of Texas at Austin and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery. A supplemental course fee of $195 applies.

description_full: What problem would you solve if you had the chance to do something about it? Students begin with needs they notice in their community or the wider world, then explore how entrepreneurs turn ideas into impact. Starting a company is one path. Creating change inside a school, business, nonprofit, or global organization is another. Working in teams, students use design thinking to generate creative solutions and improve them through conversations with real potential customers. They research their market, build a simple business model, and work through marketing, costs, and pricing. The goal is to move beyond an appealing idea: teams plan and launch a small business by the end of the academy. A UT Austin professor with real-world experience guides the work, joined by guest entrepreneurs and innovators from Austin’s startup scene. Students pitch to real entrepreneurs, listen to feedback, and strengthen their proposals before delivering a final venture pitch in the academy’s own “Shark Tank” competition. Along the way, they practice sharing decisions, leading a team, responding to setbacks, and explaining why their solution matters. This three-week full-day academy for high school students takes place at UT Austin in Austin, Texas, and is developed by the university and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery. Residential and commuter options are available. Beyond class, students build friendships, experience campus life, and gain independence alongside clearer direction about what they may want to study or pursue next. A supplemental course fee of $95 applies.

curriculum_sections.body: • Identify a real problem worth solving in your community or beyond • Use design thinking and conversations with potential customers to improve your solution • Build a simple business model with market research, marketing, costs, and pricing • Collaborate with your team to plan and launch a small business • Meet Austin entrepreneurs and innovators, pitch your idea, and apply their feedback • Craft and deliver a venture pitch in the academy’s own “Shark Tank” competition

Students should be ready to try unfamiliar approaches, talk with potential customers, collaborate on a small business, and present their ideas. The academy welcomes aspiring founders as well as students who want to bring creative problem solving, initiative, and leadership to another career or organization.

description_full: What information does a healthcare professional gather before deciding what a patient may need? Students begin with vital signs, medical-history interviews, and physical assessment. They then examine diagnostic tools used in radiology, imaging, pathology, laboratories, and clinical testing. Three simulation-lab visits make patient-care techniques concrete. Students rotate through cardiac, respiratory, and general physical assessments, then encounter intravenous access, intubation, casting, splinting, suturing, biopsy, maternal simulation, and nursery scenarios. A Heartsaver First Aid certification experience and School of Nursing tour add another view of clinical preparation and teamwork. The course also compares healthcare roles and workplaces. Students investigate medical specialties, primary care, hospitals, urgent care, rehabilitation, correctional medicine, nursing, physical therapy, occupational therapy, pharmacy, and social work. Sessions on medical-school applications, interviews, residencies, service learning, and medical humanities help students evaluate both the practical work and the training behind different paths. A book presentation connects patient care with reflection and communication. This three-week full-day academy takes place at UT Austin. Students spend the full program focused on one intensive academy. The academy is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by the University of Texas at Austin and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery. A supplemental course fee of $595 applies.

description_full: Why do some brands earn attention while others disappear into a crowded feed? Students study strategy, customer behavior, positioning, and brand voice through cases involving familiar companies. The OUTBRAND framework organizes choices about where to compete, what customers are trying to accomplish, how emotion and context affect behavior, and why social proof matters. description_full: A trace of blood, a latent fingerprint, or a single fiber can change the direction of an investigation. Students learn how forensic scientists locate, preserve, test, compare, and interpret physical evidence while protecting it from contamination. Serology exercises introduce screening for biological fluids, and DNA work examines extraction, amplification, profiles, and the role of CODIS in linking cases. The investigation expands into fingerprints, crime-scene photography, documentation, sketches, measurements, firearms evidence, bloodstain patterns, hair, fibers, paint, glass, impressions, digital evidence, drugs, and toxicology. Students practice processing porous and nonporous surfaces, lifting prints, comparing profiles, and using laboratory observations to support conclusions rather than assumptions. Teams apply these methods to two mock crime scenes. They photograph and document the scene, collect and process evidence, prepare sketches, and present their findings. Case discussions and a crime-laboratory tour connect the exercises with laboratory disciplines, expert testimony, and the legal responsibilities that follow when results are reported. description_full: Why do some people recover from setbacks more readily than others, and how do emotion, motivation, and relationships shape wellbeing? A final review brings the course’s major themes together and helps students identify questions they may want to pursue further. Personal narratives develop specificity and emotional connection. Students frame problems, establish stakes, and combine claims, warrants, evidence, and impact. Mini-debates and challenge speeches introduce ethos, pathos, and logos, while crossfire practice requires students to answer questions without losing composure or credibility. Audience-adaptation exercises ask students to present the same idea differently to parents, teachers, voters, athletes, gamers, or younger students. Impromptu prompts develop recovery skills under pressure. Each student then writes and rehearses a four-to-six-minute persuasive speech with a hook, problem, argument, solution, call to action, and memorable closing. Peer feedback and dress rehearsals lead to a final showcase. This three-week course takes place at UT Austin. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next. The program is developed by the University of Texas at Austin and offered in partnership with Summer Discovery.

Students begin by building a life-size anatomy model, then investigate how stem cells, medical devices and engineering can help repair or replace damaged tissues and organs. Design challenges make each body system concrete. Teams develop a prosthetic limb, map how 3D printing supports artificial organs and compare treatment options for kidney failure. Vision simulations and a cochlear-implant discussion add patient experience and ethics to the engineering work. Students document designs and reflections in a science journal while building a capstone proposal for a new application of regenerative medicine. The final project explains the medical need, proposed solution, possible benefits and drawbacks, and connections to areas such as cost, law, education or technology. description_full: A secret message is a mathematical puzzle with a purpose. Students trace cryptography from Caesar shifts and substitution systems to the Enigma machine and the public-key ideas that protect modern communication. Each new cipher reveals both an encoding strategy and a weakness a codebreaker can exploit. Hands-on challenges include building cipher wheels, encrypting and decrypting partner messages, using frequency analysis, and testing Vigenère and Polybius-based systems. Students connect those activities to modular arithmetic, matrices, prime factorization, number theory, and the way computers represent information. Historical cases show how cryptanalysis influenced events and how security standards change when technology advances. For the capstone, students design and analyze an original cryptographic system or complete an in-depth cryptanalysis project. They document the key, method, mathematical reasoning, strengths, limitations, and evidence from testing, then present their findings to the class. This three-week course is part of Summer Discovery’s Institute for the Gifted program on Yale University’s campus. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect active academic exploration with campus life, growing independence, new friendships, and a clearer sense of what students may want to explore next.

description_full: A human rights violation rarely involves only an offender and a victim. Students learn to examine the larger system: bystanders, potential defenders, governments, nongovernmental organizations, media and the laws or institutions that can protect rights or allow abuses to continue. The course begins with the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the ideas of universality, dignity, equality and interdependence. Students investigate current national and global cases, create concept maps and human-rights trees, analyze the role of media and study how democratic participation and social movements can create pressure for change. For the capstone, each student selects a human rights issue and maps four groups involved: the victimized, those responsible, potential benefactors and bystanders. Research develops into a position paper that defines the violation, identifies root causes and evaluates political, economic and social effects. Students then propose a sustainable youth-activism strategy, identify resources and responsible organizations, consider possible negative consequences and present the plan through video, slides, an infographic or another approved medium. This three-week course is part of Summer Discovery’s Institute for the Gifted program on Yale University’s campus. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next.

curriculum_sections.body: • Apply the Universal Declaration of Human Rights to current cases • Create concept maps and a human-rights tree linking rights to social conditions • Research victims, responsible actors, defenders and bystanders in one injustice • Evaluate how media, government and civil society shape public action • Write a position paper defining causes, effects and possible solutions • Design and present a sustainable youth-activism strategy

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Analyze a human rights issue using international principles and multiple stakeholder perspectives • Evaluate how laws, institutions, media and advocacy influence possible change • Construct and present a researched action proposal with measurable goals Students will leave with a course completion certificate, a human-rights position paper and a media presentation, plus greater clarity about further study in politics, law, international relations or advocacy.

curriculum_sections.body: This course is for high school students who have completed 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th grade and are interested in human rights, global politics, law, democracy or social change. Students should be prepared to research serious issues, compare sources, consider perspectives they may not share and present a supported position respectfully. The course expects thoughtful participation rather than a single political viewpoint. description_full: A courtroom argument must connect a claim to evidence and explain why that evidence matters. Students practice that structure through the claim, warrant, data and impact model, then learn how voice, pacing, questioning and listening affect whether an argument is understood. A scripted practice trial introduces courtroom roles and procedure. Students write openings, develop a case theory, prepare direct and cross-examinations, practice objections and compare open-ended questions with leading questions. SPAR debates require teams to argue assigned positions and respond to critique, helping students test ideas before the final trial. The capstone turns the fictional events of the book Holes into a child-labor case involving Camp Green Lake. Prosecution and defense teams research the text, organize admissible evidence, assign attorneys and witnesses, prepare questions and anticipate opposing claims. During the final mock trial, students deliver openings and closings, question witnesses, raise objections and perform their assigned courtroom roles. This three-week course is part of Summer Discovery’s Institute for the Gifted program on Yale University’s campus. The course is available to residential and commuter students. description_full: Begin with a question about medicine or public health, then work backward to determine what evidence could answer it. Students examine how medical research has developed and learn to search academic databases such as PubMed and the Cochrane Library. Literature-review activities help them compare source quality, identify gaps, and refine broad interests into focused questions and hypotheses. The course introduces PICO, quantitative and qualitative approaches, mixed methods, data collection, and basic analysis. Students consider research integrity, ethics, clinical-trial budgets, and community-engaged participatory research while testing how study design affects the strength and usefulness of a conclusion. Case studies and current health questions provide context for evaluating methods rather than treating research as a fixed recipe. This hybrid academy combines an on-campus experience with Polygence’s Core Research Program. During the campus program, each student develops a medical research proposal, abstract, and professional scientific poster, then presents the work in a symposium-style setting. Afterward, students join a virtual cohort and are matched 1:1 with a Polygence research mentor in their field of interest. Across 10 virtual sessions, the mentor helps each student continue the project at an individual pace toward a research paper, symposium presentation, podcast, or another appropriate final format. This three-week full-day academy is part of Summer Discovery’s Institute for the Gifted program on Yale University’s campus. Students spend the full program focused on one intensive academy. The academy is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next.

description_full: Microorganisms are everywhere, but their effects range from helpful to harmful. Students begin with the history of medical microbiology and the scientists whose discoveries changed how people understand infection. A handwashing and contamination investigation makes transmission visible and gives students evidence for testing a handwashing protocol. The course compares bacteria, viruses, fungi, and other microbes, then connects them to immune-system responses, infectious disease, microbiomes, and biotechnology. Students sort microbes by function, map immune cells involved in different disorders, research how a treatment affects a disease process, and communicate findings through diagrams and short presentations. For the capstone, students identify a challenge or opportunity where microorganisms play an important role. They investigate the underlying biology, current approaches, and emerging trends, then propose a scientifically grounded response. Checkpoints guide research, evidence, and presentation so the final project explains both the problem and the microbiological reasoning behind the solution. description_full: Choosing a stock is only the beginning. Students ask what makes a company worth investigating, how an investor’s goals shape strategy, and why return cannot be considered without risk, fees, and time. The course makes financial ideas visible through articles, videos, group analysis, and portfolio work. Students compare stock-picking criteria, use free screeners, examine company profiles and financial ratios, and build a hypothetical portfolio. As prices change, they calculate return on investment, review allocation choices, and consider how taxes, commissions, interest rates, and different risk profiles affect an outcome. The capstone brings those decisions into one investment presentation. Students document the companies and industries selected, explain their allocation, create a portfolio graphic, track performance, and defend the reasoning behind changes. Students compare results with classmates and revise their reasoning. The goal is not to predict the market. It is to practice making informed choices and explaining the evidence behind them. This three-week course is part of Summer Discovery’s Institute for the Gifted program on Yale University’s campus. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect active academic exploration with campus life, growing independence, new friendships, and a clearer sense of what students may want to explore next.

description_full: At the smallest scales, matter and light behave in ways that challenge everyday intuition. Students investigate the double-slit experiment, wave-particle duality, superposition, measurement, and probability through simulations and structured thought experiments such as Schrödinger’s cat. The course develops the mathematical language behind those ideas. Students work with wave functions, probability density, bra-ket notation, eigenvalues and eigenvectors, and the Schrödinger equation at an introductory level. Simulation labs let them vary conditions, observe interference patterns, and look for numerical relationships. Small-group presentations ask students to compare interpretations and explain where scientific models agree or remain debated. For the capstone, students investigate a focused question in quantum theory or technology. They gather reliable sources, use equations or visualizations where appropriate, draft an evidence-based explanation, and present conclusions. Topics may connect foundational physics to quantum computing, decoherence, or another modern application. Coursework asks students to communicate unfamiliar ideas with increasing precision. This three-week course is part of Summer Discovery’s Institute for the Gifted program on Yale University’s campus. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect focused academic work with campus life, growing independence, and clearer direction about what students may want to study or pursue next.

Course content is powered by the Network for Teaching Entrepreneurship (NFTE) and uses NFTE’s nationally recognized curriculum and Entrepreneurial Mindset framework. Students organize their idea with a Lean Business Model Canvas, conduct primary and secondary market research, define a target customer, and estimate demand. Competitive analysis, a SWOT evaluation, and human-centered design help them sharpen their value proposition. Branding and marketing workshops turn that strategy into a message customers can understand. Students then examine fixed and variable costs, pricing, revenue models, unit economics, and break-even points. Using the NFTE Business Workbook and pitch-deck framework, they assemble their research and decisions into a professional presentation. The course culminates in a Fast Pitch Challenge evaluated with NFTE’s official rubric, followed by questions and structured feedback from instructors and experienced entrepreneurs. This three-week course is part of Summer Discovery’s Institute for the Gifted program on Yale University’s campus. The course is available to residential and commuter students. Beyond class, students connect active academic exploration with campus life, growing independence, new friendships, and a clearer sense of what students may want to explore next.

curriculum_sections.title: Activities
curriculum_sections.body: • Use NFTE’s Entrepreneurial Mindset framework to identify problems and evaluate opportunities • Develop an original venture with a Lean Business Model Canvas • Conduct primary and secondary research to define a target customer • Analyze competitors, complete a SWOT review, and refine a value proposition • Calculate costs, pricing, unit economics, revenue, and a break-even point • Build a pitch deck and compete in NFTE’s Fast Pitch Challenge

curriculum_sections.title: Learning outcomes
curriculum_sections.body: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Evaluate a real-world problem as a possible business opportunity • Build and test a venture using a Lean Canvas, market research, and financial evidence • Present and defend an original business concept in NFTE’s Fast Pitch Challenge Students will leave with market research, a completed Lean Canvas, and a professional pitch deck, plus a clearer sense of which parts of entrepreneurship they may want to explore next.

curriculum_sections.title: Who should attend
curriculum_sections.body: This course is for middle school students who have completed 6th, 7th, or 8th grade and are curious about business, products, leadership, or solving problems that affect other people. It fits students who enjoy creating ideas and want to learn how NFTE’s research, business-modeling, and financial tools can make those ideas stronger. Students should be ready to collaborate, study potential customers, work with basic calculations, revise their thinking, and present to an audience. The course guides students through the NFTE process from identifying a problem to delivering a final pitch. Students must also meet the Institute for the Gifted eligibility requirements listed in the program FAQ and complete the program application.
